PasswordPolicyCatalog.Description: The number of days a password must be used before the user can change it.
PasswordPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Minimum password age policy setting determines the number of days (from 0 through 998) that a password must be used before the user is allowed to change it. It works together with Maximum password age: the minimum value must be lower than the maximum, unless the maximum is set to 0 (passwords never expire), in which case the minimum can be any value from 0 through 998.

Setting the value to 0 allows the password to be changed immediately, which is not recommended: combined with a password history requirement, it lets a user cycle through the required number of password changes in a few minutes and immediately reuse a favorite password. If an administrator sets a password for a user and wants that user to change it right away, the "User must change password at next logon" option must also be selected, otherwise the user cannot change the password until the minimum age has elapsed.

Changes to this setting take effect immediately, without a restart. The recommended value is 1 day. 

Default: 1 on domain controllers.
Default: 0 on stand-alone servers.

PasswordPolicyCatalog.Description: The number of days a password can be used before the system requires the user to change it.
PasswordPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Maximum password age policy setting determines the number of days (from 0 through 999) that a password can be used before the system requires the user to change it. Setting the value to 0 specifies that passwords never expire. When a nonzero maximum is configured, the Minimum password age value must be lower than it. Setting Maximum password age to -1 is treated the same as 0 (never expires); any other negative number is treated as Not Defined.

A short maximum password age limits the time an attacker has to compromise a password, but if set too low it can push users toward insecure habits such as writing passwords down. A value between 30 and 90 days is generally recommended, though current Microsoft guidance notes that mandated password expiration is less effective than modern mitigations such as multifactor authentication and Microsoft Entra Password Protection, and organizations that have adopted those mitigations may choose not to enforce password expiration at all.

Changes to this setting take effect immediately, without a restart. 

Default: 42.

PasswordPolicyCatalog.Description: The least number of characters a password can contain.
PasswordPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Minimum password length policy setting determines the least number of characters that a password for a user account can contain, from 0 through 14. Setting the value to 0 means no password is required at all.

Short passwords are easier to break using dictionary or brute-force attacks, while requiring very long passwords can lead to mistyped passwords, more account lockouts, and users writing passwords down. Microsoft recommends a minimum of at least 8 characters, combined with the Password must meet complexity requirements setting; a minimum length greater than 14 characters is not supported. Teaching users to rely on passphrases (short sentences) rather than single words helps them cope comfortably with longer minimums.

Changes to this setting take effect immediately, without a restart. 

Default: 7 on domain controllers.
Default: 0 on stand-alone servers.

PasswordPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether passwords must meet complexity requirements.
PasswordPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Password must meet complexity requirements policy setting determines whether passwords must satisfy a set of strong-password guidelines. When enabled, a password cannot contain the user's account name or full name, and it must contain characters from three of the following four categories: uppercase letters, lowercase letters, base-10 digits, and non-alphanumeric characters (or other Unicode letter characters that are not uppercase or lowercase). These rules are enforced by Passfilt.dll whenever a password is created or changed and cannot be modified directly, though a custom password filter can be built to enforce stricter rules.

Enabling this setting, combined with a minimum password length of 8 characters, produces a very large number of possible password combinations, making brute-force attacks much more difficult, though not impossible. If disabled or not configured, passwords are not required to meet these complexity rules, making them easier to guess or crack with common tools.

Enabling complexity requirements can increase Help Desk calls from users unfamiliar with passwords containing non-alphabetic characters. 

Default: Enabled on domain controllers.
Default: Disabled on stand-alone servers.

PasswordPolicyCatalog.Description: The number of unique new passwords that must be associated with a user account before an old password can be reused.
PasswordPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Enforce password history policy setting determines the number of unique new passwords (from 0 through 24) that must be associated with a user account before an old one can be reused. It is designed to stop users from cycling back to a favorite password as soon as they are required to change it.

A low value lets users keep reusing the same small pool of passwords; to be effective, this setting should be combined with a nonzero Minimum password age, since otherwise a user could change their password repeatedly in quick succession until they were able to reuse the original one. Microsoft recommends setting the value to 24, the maximum, together with a Maximum password age of 60 to 90 days.

Changes to this setting take effect immediately, without a restart. 

Default: 24 on domain controllers.
Default: 0 on stand-alone servers.

PasswordPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether the operating system stores passwords using reversible encryption.
PasswordPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Store passwords using reversible encryption policy setting controls whether Windows stores passwords in a form that can be decrypted, rather than only as a one-way hash. It exists to support applications that need to read back a user's plaintext password for authentication, such as the Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol (CHAP) used by some remote access and IAS connections, or Digest Authentication in Internet Information Services (IIS).

Enabling this setting is effectively equivalent to storing passwords in plaintext: an attacker able to break the reversible encryption can sign in to network resources using the compromised account. It should therefore never be enabled for all users in a domain unless a genuine application requirement outweighs the resulting loss of password protection; when it must be enabled, it is usually applied to individual user accounts rather than domain-wide.

When this setting is disabled, only newly set or changed passwords are stored using one-way encryption; passwords that were already stored reversibly remain so until they are changed.

Default: Disabled.

AccountLockoutPolicyCatalog.Description: The number of failed logon attempts that causes a user account to be locked out.
AccountLockoutPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Account lockout threshold policy setting determines the number of failed sign-in attempts (from 0 through 999) that will cause a user account to be locked out. Setting the value to 0 means the account will never be locked out regardless of how many sign-in attempts fail. A locked account remains unusable until an administrator unlocks it, or until the time set in Account lockout duration has elapsed; if the threshold is greater than 0, the lockout duration must be greater than or equal to the value configured for Reset account lockout counter after.

Limiting failed sign-in attempts makes brute-force password attacks far less effective, but a nonzero threshold can itself be abused: an attacker who knows valid account names could deliberately trigger repeated failed sign-ins to lock out large numbers of accounts as a denial-of-service attack. For this reason Microsoft describes two valid countermeasures: setting the threshold to 0 (accepting the brute-force risk but eliminating the lockout-based denial-of-service risk, appropriate only where strong password complexity and login-failure auditing are already in place), or setting it to a moderate value such as 10, which tolerates occasional mistyped passwords while still stopping automated guessing.

The built-in Administrator account is exempt from this policy so that an administrator can always sign in to remediate problems. Changes to this setting take effect immediately, without a restart. 

Default: 0.

AccountLockoutPolicyCatalog.Description: The number of minutes that must elapse after a failed logon attempt before the failed logon attempt counter is reset to 0.
AccountLockoutPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Reset account lockout counter after policy setting determines the number of minutes (from 1 through 99,999) that must elapse after a failed sign-in attempt before the failed-attempt counter is reset to 0. If Account lockout threshold is set to a value greater than 0, this reset interval must be less than or equal to the Account lockout duration.

A short reset interval lets users who mistype their password recover quickly without contacting the Help Desk, but it can also let an attacker retry passwords more frequently between lockouts. A long interval reduces that risk but increases the inconvenience, and the number of Help Desk calls, for users who lock themselves out. Microsoft's Windows security baselines recommend a value of 15 minutes, though the appropriate value depends on each organization's risk tolerance.

This setting has no effect unless Account lockout threshold is configured to a nonzero value.

Default: None, because this policy setting only has meaning when an Account lockout threshold is specified.

AccountLockoutPolicyCatalog.Description: The number of minutes a locked-out account remains locked out before automatically becoming unlocked (-1 = until an administrator unlocks it).
AccountLockoutPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Account lockout duration policy setting determines the number of minutes (from 0 through 99,999) that a locked-out account remains locked before it is automatically unlocked. Setting the value to 0 means the account stays locked until an administrator unlocks it manually. If Account lockout threshold is configured to a value greater than 0, this duration must be greater than or equal to the value set for Reset account lockout counter after.

Configuring a nonzero duration delays an attacker attempting automated password guessing, since each lockout forces a pause before further attempts against that account can resume; combined with Account lockout threshold, this makes brute-force attacks considerably harder. Microsoft recommends a duration of approximately 15 minutes for most environments.

Setting the duration to 0 maximizes protection against repeated guessing but increases the number of Help Desk requests to unlock accounts that were locked by mistake, since no automatic recovery occurs. 

Default: None, because this policy setting only has meaning when an Account lockout threshold is specified.

AccountLockoutPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether the built-in Administrator account is subject to account lockout policy.
AccountLockoutPolicyCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the built-in Administrator account is subject to account lockout policy.

Default Value: Disabled.

OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Description: Determines whether to disconnect users who are connected outside their user account access hours.
OtherSystemAccessCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Force logoff when logon hours expire
OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether to disconnect users who remain connected to the local device outside the hours during which their account is permitted to sign in. It affects only the Server Message Block (SMB) component—that is, network sessions such as file and print sharing—and does not apply to administrator accounts.

When enabled, active SMB client sessions are forcibly disconnected as soon as the user's allowed logon hours expire, and the user cannot sign in again until their next scheduled access window begins. When disabled, an already-established SMB session is allowed to continue even after the user's logon hours have expired.

This setting behaves as an account policy, and for domain accounts there can be only one effective account policy, defined in the Default Domain Policy and enforced by the domain's domain controllers; a domain controller always applies the Default Domain Policy's account policy even if a different one is linked to the organizational unit containing it. Changes take effect immediately, without a restart. Default value: Disabled for the Default Domain Policy and for all effective settings.

OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Description: Determines whether the local built-in Administrator account is enabled.
OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the local Administrator account is enabled or disabled.

Notes : If you try to reenable the Administrator account after it has been disabled, and if the current Administrator password does not meet the password requirements, you cannot reenable the account. In this case, an alternative member of the Administrators group must reset the password on the Administrator account. For information about how to reset a password, see To reset a password.
Disabling the Administrator account can become a maintenance issue under certain circumstances. 

Under Safe Mode boot, the disabled Administrator account will only be enabled if the machine is non-domain joined and there are no other local active administrator accounts.  If the computer is domain joined the disabled administrator will not be enabled.

Default: Disabled.

OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Description: Determines whether the local built-in Guest account is enabled.
OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines if the Guest account is enabled or disabled.

Note: If the Guest account is disabled and the security option Network Access: Sharing and Security Model for local accounts is set to Guest Only, network logons, such as those performed by the Microsoft Network Server (SMB Service), will fail.

Default: Disabled.

OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Description: The name associated with the local Administrator account (well-known SID).
OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether a different account name is associated with the security identifier (SID) for the account Administrator. Renaming the well-known Administrator account makes it slightly more difficult for unauthorized persons to guess this privileged user name and password combination.

Default: Administrator.

OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Description: The name associated with the local Guest account (well-known SID).
OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether a different account name is associated with the security identifier (SID) for the account "Guest." Renaming the well-known Guest account makes it slightly more difficult for unauthorized persons to guess this user name and password combination.

Default: Guest.

OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Description: Determines whether an anonymous user can request SID attributes for another user, or use a SID to obtain its corresponding user name.
OtherSystemAccessCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Allow anonymous SID/Name translation
OtherSystemAccessCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether an anonymous user is allowed to request the security identifier (SID) attributes of another user, or the name corresponding to a known SID. It governs both SID-to-name and name-to-SID translation for unauthenticated network connections.

When enabled, an anonymous user who knows the well-known SID of the built-in Administrators group can query a computer that has this setting enabled to recover the real account name of the built-in Administrator account—even if that account has been renamed—and then use that name to mount a brute-force password-guessing attack. When disabled, anonymous SID/name and name/SID translation requests are refused, closing off that reconnaissance path. Misconfiguring this setting is a common source of unexpected data-access problems, so changes should be tested before wide deployment.

Default : workstations and member servers: Disabled.
Default : domain controllers running Windows Server 2008 or later: Disabled.
Default : domain controllers running Windows Server 2003 R2 or earlier: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Accounts: Limit local account use of blank passwords to console logon only
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether local accounts with blank passwords can be used to log on from locations other than the physical console.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether local accounts that are not password protected can be used to log on from locations other than the physical computer console. If enabled, local accounts that are not password protected will only be able to log on at the computer's keyboard.

Warning: Computers that are not in physically secure locations should always enforce strong password policies for all local user accounts. Otherwise, anyone with physical access to the computer can log on by using a user account that does not have a password. This is especially important for portable computers.
If you apply this security policy to the Everyone group, no one will be able to log on through Remote Desktop Services.

Notes This setting does not affect logons that use domain accounts.
It is possible for applications that use remote interactive logons to bypass this setting.

Note: Remote Desktop Services was called Terminal Services in previous versions of Windows Server.

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Audit: Force audit policy subcategory settings to override audit policy category settings
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether audit policy subcategory settings (Windows Vista or later) override audit policy category settings.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Windows Vista and later versions of Windows allow audit policy to be managed in a more precise way using audit policy subcategories.  Setting audit policy at the category level will override the new subcategory audit policy feature.  
Group Policy only allows audit policy to be set at the category level, and existing group policy may override the subcategory settings of new machines as they are joined to the domain or upgraded to Windows Vista or later versions.  

To allow audit policy to be managed using subcategories without requiring a change to Group Policy, there is a new registry value in Windows Vista and later versions, SCENoApplyLegacyAuditPolicy, which prevents the application of category-level audit policy from Group Policy and from the Local Security Policy administrative tool.

If the category level audit policy set here is not consistent with the events that are currently being generated, the cause might be that this registry key is set.

Default: Enabled

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Audit: Audit the use of Backup and Restore privilege
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether to audit the use of all user rights, including Backup and Restore, when the Audit privilege use policy setting is configured.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines whether to audit the use of all user rights, including Backup and Restore, when the Audit privilege use policy setting is configured. Enabling both policy settings generates an audit event for every file that is backed up or restored. If Audit privilege use is enabled but this setting is disabled, backup and restore rights are not audited even though other privilege use is.

When the backup and restore function is used, it creates a copy of the file system that is identical to the target of the backup. Making regular backup and restore volumes is an important part of an incident response plan; however, a malicious user could use a legitimate backup copy to gain access to information or to impersonate a legitimate network resource to compromise the enterprise.

Enabling this policy setting can generate a large number of security events, which might cause servers to respond slowly and force the security log to record numerous events of little significance; if the security event log size is increased to reduce the chances of a shutdown, an excessively large log file may itself affect system performance. For this reason it is generally left Disabled, using the advanced audit policy Audit Sensitive Privilege Use to help manage the number of events generated instead, if this level of tracking is needed.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Audit: Shut down system immediately if unable to log security audits
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the system shuts down if it is unable to log security events, for any reason.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the system shuts down if it is unable to log security events.

If this security setting is enabled, it causes the system to stop if a security audit cannot be logged for any reason. Typically, an event fails to be logged when the security audit log is full and the retention method that is specified for the security log is either Do Not Overwrite Events or Overwrite Events by Days.

If the security log is full and an existing entry cannot be overwritten, and this security option is enabled, the following Stop error appears:

STOP: C0000244 {Audit Failed}
An attempt to generate a security audit failed.
To recover, an administrator must log on, archive the log (optional), clear the log, and reset this option as desired. Until this security setting is reset, no users, other than a member of the Administrators group will be able to log on to the system, even if the security log is not full.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Devices: Prevent users from installing printer drivers
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines who is allowed to install a printer driver as part of connecting to a shared printer.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
For a computer to print to a shared printer, the driver for that shared printer must be installed on the local computer. This security setting determines who is allowed to install a printer driver as part of connecting to a shared printer. If this setting is enabled, only Administrators can install a printer driver as part of connecting to a shared printer. If this setting is disabled, any user can install a printer driver as part of connecting to a shared printer.

Default : Enabled on servers.
Default : Disabled on workstations.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain controller: Allow server operators to schedule tasks
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether Server Operators are allowed to submit jobs by means of the AT schedule facility, on a domain controller.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines if Server Operators are allowed to submit jobs by means of the AT schedule facility.

Note: This security setting only affects the AT schedule facility; it does not affect the Task Scheduler facility.

Default: This policy is not defined, which means that the system treats it as disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain controller: LDAP server channel binding token requirements
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the LDAP server enforces validation of channel binding tokens on incoming connections.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the LDAP server enforces validation of Channel Binding Tokens received in LDAP bind requests sent over LDAPS connections, as follows:

Never: No channel binding validation is performed. This is the behavior of all servers that have not been updated.

When supported: Clients that advertise support for Channel Binding Tokens must provide the correct token when authenticating over TLS/SSL connections; clients that do not advertise such support and/or do not use TLS/SSL connections are not impacted. This is an intermediate option that allows for application compatibility.

Always: All clients must provide channel binding information over LDAPS. The server rejects LDAPS authentication requests from clients that do not do so.

Default: This policy is not defined, which has the same effect as When Supported.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the LDAP server requires signing to be negotiated with LDAP clients.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the LDAP server requires signing to be negotiated with LDAP clients, as follows:

None: Data signing is not required in order to bind with the server. If the client requests data signing, the server supports it.
Require signature: Unless TLS\SSL is being used, the LDAP data signing option must be negotiated.

Default: This policy is not defined, which has the same effect as None.

Caution :If you set the server to Require Signature, you must also set the client. Not setting the client results in loss of connection with the server.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements Enforcement
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the domain controller enforces LDAP signing independently of the Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements policy.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting, introduced in Windows Server 2025, determines whether the domain controller enforces LDAP signing requirements independently of the Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements policy - it exists so that new Active Directory deployments get a secure-by-default LDAP signing posture without an administrator having to explicitly configure the older policy.

Enabled: LDAP signing is enforced regardless of what is configured in Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements.

Disabled: The domain controller falls back to whatever is configured in Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements.

When both this policy and Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements are configured, this policy's setting takes precedence and the other is ignored. Domain controllers upgraded from an earlier Windows Server version keep whatever LDAP signing configuration they already had, so this new enforcement default only affects deployments that start on Windows Server 2025 or later.

Default: Not Configured, which has the same effect as Enabled on Windows Server 2025 and later.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain controller: Refuse machine account password changes
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether domain controllers refuse requests from domain members to change the computer account password.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether domain controllers will refuse requests from member computers to change computer account passwords. By default, member computers change their computer account passwords every 30 days. If enabled, the domain controller will refuse computer account password change requests.

If it is enabled, this setting does not allow a domain controller to accept any changes to a computer account's password.

Default: This policy is not defined, which means that the system treats it as Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain controller: Refuse setting default machine account password
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether domain controllers refuse setting a computer account's password to the predictable default value derived from its account name.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting, introduced in Windows Server 2025, determines whether domain controllers refuse setting a computer account's password to its default machine account password upon creation. When a computer account is first created (for example a pre-staged computer object, or one created but not yet joined), its initial password is a predictable value derived from the account name rather than a random secret.

If an attacker can predict or already knows this default password for an account that has not yet completed a real domain join, they could authenticate as that computer account and take it over before the legitimate machine ever sets a real password on it. If this setting is enabled, the domain controller refuses any attempt to (re-)set a computer account's password to that predictable default value, closing off this avenue.

This setting only affects domain controllers running Windows Server 2025 or later; it has no effect on earlier domain controllers, and computer accounts that already have such a default password in place before this setting is enabled are not retroactively affected.

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether all secure channel traffic initiated by this domain member must be signed or encrypted.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether all secure channel traffic initiated by the domain member must be signed or encrypted.

When a computer joins a domain, a computer account is created. After that, when the system starts, it uses the computer account password to create a secure channel with a domain controller for its domain. This secure channel is used to perform operations such as NTLM pass through authentication, LSA SID/name Lookup etc.

This setting determines whether or not all secure channel traffic initiated by the domain member meets minimum security requirements. Specifically it determines whether all secure channel traffic initiated by the domain member must be signed or encrypted. If this policy is enabled, then the secure channel will not be established unless either signing or encryption of all secure channel traffic is negotiated. If this policy is disabled, then encryption and signing of all secure channel traffic is negotiated with the Domain Controller in which case the level of signing and encryption depends on the version of the Domain Controller and the settings of the following two policies:

Domain member: Digitally encrypt secure channel data (when possible)
Domain member: Digitally sign secure channel data (when possible)

Notes: If this policy is enabled, the policy Domain member: Digitally sign secure channel data (when possible) is assumed to be enabled regardless of its current setting. This ensures that the domain member attempts to negotiate at least signing of the secure channel traffic.
Logon information transmitted over the secure channel is always encrypted regardless of whether encryption of ALL other secure channel traffic is negotiated or not.

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain member: Digitally encrypt secure channel data (when possible)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a domain member attempts to negotiate encryption for all secure channel traffic that it initiates.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether a domain member attempts to negotiate encryption for all secure channel traffic that it initiates.

When a computer joins a domain, a computer account is created. After that, when the system starts, it uses the computer account password to create a secure channel with a domain controller for its domain. This secure channel is used to perform operations such as NTLM pass-through authentication, LSA SID/name Lookup etc.

This setting determines whether or not the domain member attempts to negotiate encryption for all secure channel traffic that it initiates. If enabled, the domain member will request encryption of all secure channel traffic. If the domain controller supports encryption of all secure channel traffic, then all secure channel traffic will be encrypted. Otherwise only logon information transmitted over the secure channel will be encrypted. If this setting is disabled, then the domain member will not attempt to negotiate secure channel encryption.

Important There is no known reason for disabling this setting. Besides unnecessarily reducing the potential confidentiality level of the secure channel, disabling this setting may unnecessarily reduce secure channel throughput, because concurrent API calls that use the secure channel are only possible when the secure channel is signed or encrypted.

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain member: Digitally sign secure channel data (when possible)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a domain member attempts to negotiate signing for all secure channel traffic that it initiates.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether a domain member attempts to negotiate signing for all secure channel traffic that it initiates.

When a computer joins a domain, a computer account is created. After that, when the system starts, it uses the computer account password to create a secure channel with a domain controller for its domain. This secure channel is used to perform operations such as NTLM pass through authentication, LSA SID/name Lookup etc.

This setting determines whether or not the domain member attempts to negotiate signing for all secure channel traffic that it initiates. If enabled, the domain member will request signing of all secure channel traffic. If the Domain Controller supports signing of all secure channel traffic, then all secure channel traffic will be signed which ensures that it cannot be tampered with in transit.

Notes: If the policy Domain member: Digitally encrypt or sign secure channel data (always) is enabled, then this policy is assumed to be enabled regardless of its current setting.
Domain controllers are also domain members and establish secure channels with other domain controllers in the same domain as well as domain controllers in trusted domains.

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain member: Disable machine account password changes
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a domain member periodically changes its computer account password.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Determines whether a domain member periodically changes its computer account password. If this setting is enabled, the domain member does not attempt to change its computer account password. If this setting is disabled, the domain member attempts to change its computer account password as specified by the setting for Domain Member: Maximum age for machine account password, which by default is every 30 days.

Notes : This security setting should not be enabled. Computer account passwords are used to establish secure channel communications between members and domain controllers and, within the domain, between the domain controllers themselves. Once it is established, the secure channel is used to transmit sensitive information that is necessary for making authentication and authorization decisions.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain member: Maximum machine account password age (days)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines the maximum allowable age (in days) for a domain member's computer account password.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines how often a domain member will attempt to change its computer account password.

Important : This setting applies to Windows 2000 computers, but it is not available through the Security Configuration Manager tools on these computers.

Default: 30 days.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain member: Require strong (Windows 2000 or later) session key
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a secure channel can only be established with a domain controller capable of encrypting the secure channel with a strong session key.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines whether a secure channel can be established with a domain controller that isn't capable of encrypting secure channel traffic with a strong, 128-bit session key. Whenever possible, you should take advantage of these stronger session keys to help protect secure channel communications from eavesdropping and session-hijacking network attacks.

If you enable this setting on a member workstation or server, all domain controllers in the domain that the member belongs to must be capable of encrypting secure channel data with a strong, 128-bit key, meaning they must be running at least Windows 2000 Server; all outgoing secure channel traffic then requires a strong encryption key, and a secure channel can't be established with a domain controller that doesn't support it. If you disable this setting, 64-bit session keys are allowed and key strength is negotiated.

Only enable this setting if the domain controllers in all trusted domains support strong keys, since devices that don't support this setting can't join domains where it's enabled. No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Disabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings.

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Do not require CTRL+ALT+DEL
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether users must press CTRL+ALT+DEL before they log on.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether pressing CTRL+ALT+DEL is required before a user can log on.

If this policy is enabled on a computer, a user is not required to press CTRL+ALT+DEL to log on. Not having to press CTRL+ALT+DEL leaves users susceptible to attacks that attempt to intercept the users' passwords. Requiring CTRL+ALT+DEL before users log on ensures that users are communicating by means of a trusted path when entering their passwords.

If this policy is disabled, any user is required to press CTRL+ALT+DEL before logging on to Windows.

Default : on domain-computers Enabled At least Windows  8.
Default : on stand-alone computers Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Don't display last signed-in
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the name of the last user to log on is displayed on the logon screen.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the Windows sign-in screen will show the username of the last person who signed in on this PC.

If this policy is enabled, the username will not be shown.

If this policy is disabled, the username will be shown.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Machine inactivity limit (seconds)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Number of seconds of inactivity before the screen saver/lock screen activates automatically (0 = disabled).
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Windows notices inactivity of a logon session, and if the amount of inactive time exceeds the inactivity limit, then the screen saver will run, locking the session.

Default: not enforced.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache (in case domain controller is not available)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Number of unique previous logons for which credentials are cached locally (0 to 50), stored as text.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines whether a user can sign in to a Windows domain by using cached account information: sign-in information for domain accounts can be cached locally so that, if a domain controller can't be contacted on subsequent logons, a user can still sign in. This policy setting determines the number of unique users whose sign-in information is cached locally; if the value is 10, the server caches sign-in information for 10 users, and when an 11th user signs in, the server overwrites the oldest cached sign-in session.

If a domain controller is unavailable and a user's sign-in information is cached, the user is told they've been signed in using cached account information and that changes to their profile since their last logon might not be available; if it isn't cached, the user is told the system can't log them on because the domain isn't available. Sign-in credentials of users who access the server console are cached on that server; a malicious user who can access the file system could locate this cached information and attempt a brute-force attack to determine passwords, but Windows mitigates this by encrypting the information and spreading the cached credentials across the system's registries in numerous physical locations. The cached account information doesn't expire, but can get overwritten as described.

The possible value is a user-defined number from 0 through 50, or Not defined; the Windows security baselines don't recommend configuring this setting. No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect.

Default: Windows Server 2008: 25
Default: All Other Versions: 10

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Prompt user to change password before expiration (days)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Number of days in advance to warn the user that their password is about to expire.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Determines how far in advance (in days) users are warned that their password is about to expire. With this advance warning, the user has time to construct a password that is sufficiently strong.

Default: 5 days.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Require Domain Controller Authentication to unlock workstation
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a domain controller must be contacted to unlock a computer that was locked with a domain account.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Unlocking a locked device requires sign-in information. For domain accounts, this policy setting determines whether it's necessary to contact a domain controller to unlock a device. Enabling this policy setting requires a domain controller to authenticate the domain account being used to unlock the device; disabling it allows a user to unlock the device without the computer verifying the sign-in information with a domain controller — however, if Interactive logon: Number of previous logons to cache is set to a value greater than zero, the user's cached credentials will be used to unlock the system.

The device caches locally in memory the credentials of any users who have been authenticated, and uses these cached credentials to authenticate anyone who attempts to unlock the console. When cached credentials are used, any changes recently made to the account — such as user rights assignments, account lockout, or the account being disabled — aren't considered or applied after this authentication process: user rights aren't updated, and disabled accounts are still able to unlock the console.

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Smart card removal behavior

Choices.DisplayName: Disconnect if a remote Remote Desktop Services session

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines what happens when the smart card for a logged-on user is removed from the smart card reader.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines what happens when the smart card for a signed-in user is removed from the smart card reader. If smart cards are used for authentication, the device should automatically lock itself when the card is removed, so that a user who forgets to manually lock their device when leaving doesn't leave it open to a malicious user. This policy depends on the Smart Card Removal Policy service, which must be running for the policy to take effect, so it's recommended to set the service's startup type to Automatic.

If you select Lock Workstation, the workstation locks when the smart card is removed, letting the user leave the area with their card while maintaining a protected session — this is the recommended setting. If you select Force Logoff, the user is automatically logged off when the card is removed — useful for a device deployed as a public access point such as a kiosk — and must reinsert the card and re-enter the PIN upon returning. Disconnect if a Remote Desktop Services session disconnects the remote session without logging the user off, so the session can be resumed later from another smart-card-equipped computer (for a local session, this option behaves identically to Lock Workstation); finally, No Action has no effect when the card is removed.

Default: This policy is not defined, which means that the system treats it as No action.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Message title for users attempting to log on
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Title displayed in the title bar of the window that contains the logon message.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting allows the specification of a title to appear in the title bar of the window that contains the Interactive logon: Message text for users attempting to log on.

Default: No message.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Message text for users attempting to log on
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Text displayed to users when they log on, before they can log on to the system.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting specifies a text message that is displayed to users when they log on.

This text is often used for legal reasons, for example, to warn users about the ramifications of misusing company information or to warn them that their actions may be audited.

Default: No message.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether SMB packet signing must be negotiated before further communication with an SMB server is permitted.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
The Server Message Block (SMB) protocol provides the basis for file and print sharing and many other networking operations, such as remote Windows administration. To prevent man-in-the-middle attacks that modify SMB packets in transit, SMB supports digital signing of packets; implementing digital signatures in high-security networks helps prevent impersonation of client computers and servers, known as "session hijacking." Beginning with SMBv2 clients and servers, signing can be either required or not required. If this policy setting is enabled, SMBv2 clients will digitally sign all packets; a separate setting, Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always), determines whether signing is required on the server side for SMBv3 and SMBv2.

Negotiation occurs between the SMB client and server to decide whether signing will be used: if the client requires signing, communication is always signed regardless of whether the server requires it; if the client doesn't require it, communication is signed by default with a domain controller, but not with other SMB traffic. Important: Microsoft doesn't recommend using the "sign if the server/client agrees" policy settings, nor the EnableSecuritySignature registry values, which only affect SMBv1 behavior (a deprecated protocol no longer installed by default since Windows 10 version 1709); they can be effectively replaced by this "always" setting or by the RequireSecuritySignature registry value.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (if server agrees)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the SMB client attempts to negotiate SMB packet signing with an SMB server that agrees to it.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
The SMB protocol provides the basis for file and print sharing and many other networking operations. To prevent man-in-the-middle attacks that modify SMB packets in transit, SMB supports digital signing of packets; this policy setting determines whether packet signing must be negotiated before communication with the Server service is allowed. If server-side SMB signing is required, a client computer won't be able to establish a session with that server unless client-side SMB signing is enabled; by default, client-side signing is enabled on workstations, servers, and domain controllers. Conversely, if client-side signing is required, the client won't be able to establish a session with servers where packet signing isn't enabled; by default, server-side signing is enabled only on domain controllers.

If you enable this setting ("if server agrees"), SMB packet signing will be negotiated with client computers for which it's enabled. Using SMB packet signing can cause performance degradation of up to 15% on file service transactions. Three related settings jointly determine SMB signing requirements: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always), Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always), and Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (if client agrees).

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Microsoft network client: Send unencrypted password to third-party SMB servers
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the SMB redirector sends plaintext passwords when authenticating to third-party SMB servers that do not support password encryption.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
The SMB protocol provides the basis for file and print sharing and many other networking operations, such as remote Windows administration. This policy setting allows or prevents the SMB redirector from sending plaintext passwords to a non-Microsoft server service that doesn't support password encryption during authentication.

If you enable this setting, the SMB redirector is allowed to send plaintext passwords to a non-Microsoft server service that doesn't support encryption, which lets the server transmit those plaintext passwords across the network to other computers, potentially without benefiting from the SMB security mechanisms included since Windows Server 2003. If you disable this setting, the SMB redirector only sends encrypted passwords to non-Microsoft SMB server services; if those services don't support password encryption, the authentication request fails — some older applications may then no longer be able to communicate with the organization's servers through SMB.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Microsoft network server: Amount of idle time required before suspending session (minutes)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Number of minutes of continuous idle time that must pass in an SMB session before the session is suspended due to inactivity.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Each Server Message Block (SMB) session consumes server resources; establishing numerous null sessions causes the server to slow down or possibly fail. A malicious user might repeatedly establish SMB sessions until the server's SMB services become slow or unresponsive. This policy setting determines the amount of continuous idle time that must pass in an SMB session before the session is suspended due to inactivity; the session is automatically reestablished when client device activity resumes.

The possible value is a user-defined number of minutes from 0 through 99,999: a value of 0 disconnects an idle session as quickly as is reasonably possible, while the maximum value of 99,999 (about 208 days) effectively disables the policy. It's advisable to set this policy to 15 minutes; there's little impact because SMB sessions will be reestablished automatically if the client resumes activity.

Default:This policy is not defined, which means that the system treats it as 15 minutes for servers and undefined for workstation

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether SMB packet signing must be negotiated before further communication with an SMB client is permitted.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
The SMB protocol provides the basis for file and print sharing and many other networking operations, such as remote Windows administration. To prevent man-in-the-middle attacks that modify SMB packets in transit, SMB supports digital signing of packets; implementing digital signatures in high-security networks helps prevent session hijacking. Beginning with SMBv2 clients and servers, signing can be either required or not required; if this policy setting is enabled, the server will require signing of all packets for SMBv3 and SMBv2, with a separate client-side setting determining the equivalent behavior for clients.

Negotiation occurs between the SMB client and server: if the server requires signing, communication is always signed regardless of the client's setting; if the server doesn't require it, communication is signed by default for domain controller SMB traffic, but not for other SMB traffic. Important: Microsoft doesn't recommend using the "sign if client/server agrees" policy settings, nor the EnableSecuritySignature registry values, which only affect SMBv1 behavior (a deprecated protocol no longer installed by default since Windows 10 version 1709); they can be effectively replaced by this "always" setting or by the RequireSecuritySignature registry value.

Default: Disabled for member servers.
Default: Enabled for domain controllers.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (if client agrees)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the SMB server negotiates SMB packet signing with clients that request it.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
The SMB protocol provides the basis for file and print sharing and many other networking operations. To prevent man-in-the-middle attacks that modify SMB packets in transit, SMB supports digital signing of packets; this policy setting determines whether SMB packet signing must be negotiated before communication with the Server service is allowed. For this policy to take effect on computers running Windows 2000, client-side signing must also be enabled via Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (if server agrees); devices with this server-side policy set won't be able to communicate with clients that don't have client-side signing enabled. By default, server-side signing is enabled only on domain controllers.

If you enable this setting ("if client agrees"), SMB packet signing will be negotiated with clients for which SMB signing is enabled; using packet signing can cause performance degradation of up to 15% on file service transactions. Three related settings jointly determine SMB signing requirements: Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (always), Microsoft network server: Digitally sign communications (always), and Microsoft network client: Digitally sign communications (if server agrees).

Default: Enabled on domain controllers only.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Microsoft network server: Disconnect clients when logon hours expire
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether SMB sessions are forcibly disconnected when a client's valid logon hours expire.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting enables or disables the forced disconnection of users who are connected to the local device outside their user account's valid sign-in hours, and it affects the SMB component. If you enable this policy setting, client computer sessions with the SMB service are forcibly disconnected when the client's sign-in hours expire; if sign-in hours aren't used in your organization, enabling this policy setting has no impact.

If you disable or do not configure this policy setting, established client device sessions are maintained after the client device's sign-in hours expire. If your organization configures sign-in hours for users, it's advisable to enable this policy setting, or else users who shouldn't have access to network resources outside of their sign-in hours can continue to use those resources with sessions established during allowed hours. It's also advisable to enable Network security: Force logoff when logon hours expire alongside this setting.

Default on Windows Vista and above: Enabled.
Default on Windows XP: Disabled

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Microsoft network server: Server SPN target name validation level
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines the level of validation a SMB server performs on the service principal name (SPN) provided by the SMB client when establishing a session.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting controls the level of validation that a server with shared folders or printers performs on the service principal name (SPN) provided by the client device when it establishes a session using the SMB protocol. This validation level can help prevent a class of attacks against SMB services known as SMB relay attacks; this setting affects both SMB1 and SMB2. Servers that use SMB provide networked client devices access to their file systems and other resources such as printers, and typically validate access using NT Domain authentication (NTLMv1/NTLMv2) and the Kerberos protocol.

Three validation levels are possible: Off, where the SPN provided by the client isn't required or validated (the default value); Accept if provided by client, where the SMB server validates the SPN provided by the client, if any, and allows the session if it matches the server's own list of SPNs, denying the session if there's a mismatch; and Required from client, where the SMB client must send a matching SPN when establishing the session, with the session denied if no SPN is provided or the SPN doesn't match.

This setting affects server-side SMB behavior and should be carefully evaluated and tested before deployment, because since the SMB protocol is widely deployed, setting this option to Accept if provided by client or Required from client will prevent some clients from successfully authenticating to some servers in your environment. No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Off in the Default Domain Policy, the Default Domain Controller Policy, and on Stand-Alone Server effective settings; on domain controllers, member servers, and client computers, the validation level check isn't implemented by default.

Default: Off

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines what additional permissions are granted for anonymous connections to the computer, preventing enumeration of SAM accounts.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines which other permissions will be assigned for anonymous connections to the device. Windows allows anonymous users to perform certain activities, such as enumerating the names of domain accounts and network shares, which can be convenient, for example, when an administrator wants to give access to users in a trusted domain that doesn't maintain a reciprocal trust. This policy setting has no impact on domain controllers.

If you enable this setting, no other permissions can be assigned by the administrator for anonymous connections to the device, and anonymous connections rely solely on default permissions; this prevents an unauthorized user from anonymously listing account names to attempt social engineering attacks or guess passwords. Even with this policy setting enabled, anonymous users will still have access to resources with permissions that explicitly include the built-in group ANONYMOUS LOGON (on systems earlier than Windows Server 2008 and Windows Vista).

Default on workstations: Enabled.
Default on server:Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares is allowed, in addition to the default permissions of anonymous users.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines which other permissions will be assigned for anonymous connections to the device. Windows allows anonymous users to perform certain activities, such as enumerating the names of domain accounts and network shares, which can be convenient for giving access to users in a trusted domain that doesn't maintain a reciprocal trust; however, even with this policy setting enabled, anonymous users will have access to resources with permissions that explicitly include the built-in group ANONYMOUS LOGON. This policy setting has no impact on domain controllers, and misuse of it is a common error that can cause data loss or problems with data access or security.

If you enable this setting, no other permissions can be assigned by the administrator for anonymous connections to the device, and anonymous connections rely solely on default permissions; without this setting, an unauthorized user could anonymously list account names and shared resources and use the information to attempt to guess passwords or perform social-engineering attacks.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Do not allow storage of passwords and credentials for network authentication
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether Credential Manager saves passwords and credentials for later use when it gains domain authentication.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether Credential Manager saves passwords and credentials for later use when it gains domain authentication. It's recommended practice to disable the Windows operating system's ability to cache credentials on any device where they aren't needed; cached credentials are designed primarily for laptops that require domain credentials when disconnected from the domain.

If you enable this setting, Credential Manager doesn't store passwords and credentials on the device, which prevents malware that a user unknowingly runs from reading cached passwords and forwarding them to another unauthorized user. If you disable it, Credential Manager stores passwords and credentials on the computer for later use for domain authentication. To limit the number of cached domain credentials stored on the computer, you can also set the cachedlogonscount registry entry (0 to 50, defaulting to 10 logons, 25 since Windows Server 2008); the ReportDC registry entry can notify you of a sign-in that uses cached domain credentials when a domain controller is unavailable.

A restart of the device is required before a change to this policy becomes effective, whether saved locally or distributed through Group Policy. 

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Let Everyone permissions apply to anonymous users
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines what additional permissions are granted for anonymous connections to the computer, including membership in the Everyone group.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines what other permissions are granted for anonymous connections to the device. By default, the token created for an anonymous connection doesn't include the Everyone security identifier (SID), so permissions assigned to the Everyone group don't apply to anonymous users.

If you enable this setting, the Everyone SID is added to the token created for anonymous connections, and anonymous users can then access any resource for which the Everyone group has been assigned permissions — which would let an unauthorized user anonymously list account names and shared resources to attempt to guess passwords, perform social engineering attacks, or launch denial-of-service attacks. If you disable this setting (recommended), the Everyone SID is removed from the token created for anonymous connections; anonymous users can still enumerate the names of domain accounts and network shares, which remains convenient when an administrator wants to grant access to users in a trusted domain that doesn't maintain a reciprocal trust.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Disabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings; this default configuration has no impact.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Named pipes that can be accessed anonymously
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines which communication sessions (named pipes, comma-separated) will have attributes and permissions that allow anonymous access.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines which communication sessions, or named pipes, have attributes and permissions that allow anonymous access. Restricting access over named pipes such as COMNAP and LOCATOR helps prevent unauthorized access to the network; these pipes — including COMNAP, COMNODE, SQL\QUERY, SPOOLSS, EPMAPPER, LOCATOR, TrlWks, and TrkSvr — were granted anonymous access in earlier versions of Windows, and some legacy applications may still rely on them.

The possible value is a user-defined list of named pipes, or Not defined. It's advisable to set this policy to a null value — that is, enable the setting but don't enter any named pipes in the text box — which disables null session access over named pipes; applications that rely on this feature or on unauthenticated access to named pipes will then no longer function, which can also break trust between Windows Server 2003 domains in a mixed-mode environment. Note: for this policy setting to take effect, you must also enable Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value contains Netlogon, samr, lsarpc in the Default Domain Controller Policy and on domain controller effective settings, and Null on Stand-Alone Server effective settings; it is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and on Member Server and Client Computer effective settings.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Remotely accessible registry paths
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines which registry paths (comma-separated) are accessible over the network, regardless of the users or groups listed in the access control list of the winreg registry key.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines which registry paths are accessible remotely when an application or process references the WinReg key to determine access permissions. The registry is a database for device configuration information, much of which is sensitive; a malicious user can use it to facilitate unauthorized activities, but suitable access control lists (ACLs) are assigned throughout the registry to help protect it from access by unauthorized users. To allow remote access, the Remote Registry service must also be enabled.

The possible value is a user-defined list of paths, or Not defined. It's advisable to set this policy to a null value — enable the setting but don't enter any paths in the text box — keeping in mind that remote management tools such as the Microsoft Baseline Security Analyzer and Configuration Manager require remote access to the registry: removing the default paths from the list of accessible ones could cause such tools to fail.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value corresponds to the combination of the System\CurrentControlSet\Control\ProductOptions, System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Server Applications, and Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion keys on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings; it is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Remotely accessible registry paths and sub-paths
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines which registry paths and sub-paths (comma-separated) are accessible over the network.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines which registry paths and subpaths are accessible remotely when an application or process references the WinReg key to determine access permissions. The registry is a database for device configuration information, much of which is sensitive; this risk is reduced by the fact that the default ACLs assigned throughout the registry are fairly restrictive. To allow remote access, the Remote Registry service must also be enabled.

The possible value is a user-defined list of paths, or Not defined. It's advisable to set this policy to a null value — enable the setting but don't enter any paths in the text box — since remote management tools such as MBSA and Configuration Manager require remote access to the registry; removing the default paths from the list could cause such tools to fail.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value corresponds to the combination of the System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Printers, System\CurrentControlSet\Services\Eventlog, Software\Microsoft\OLAP Server, Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Print, Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows, System\CurrentControlSet\Control\ContentIndex, System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server (and its UserConfig and DefaultUserConfiguration subkeys), Software\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Perflib, and System\CurrentControlSet\Services\SysmonLog keys, on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings; it is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether anonymous access to shares and named pipes is restricted to those explicitly listed.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting enables or disables the restriction of anonymous access to only those shared folders and pipes that are named in the Network access: Named pipes that can be accessed anonymously and Network access: Shares that can be accessed anonymously settings. It controls null session access to shared folders by adding the RestrictNullSessAccess value (with data 1) to the registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManServer\Parameters; this registry value toggles null session shared folders on or off to determine whether the Server service restricts unauthenticated clients' access to named resources. Null sessions are a weakness that can be exploited through the various shared folders on devices in your environment.

It's advisable to set this policy to Enabled: enabling it restricts null session access for unauthenticated users to all server pipes and shared folders except those listed in the NullSessionPipes and NullSessionShares registry entries.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings, and Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Security descriptor (SDDL) string determining who is allowed to make remote calls to the Security Account Manager (SAM).
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Restrict clients allowed to make remote calls to SAM
Network access: Shares that can be accessed anonymously
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines which network shares (comma-separated) can be accessed by anonymous users.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines which shared folders can be accessed by anonymous users. The possible value is a user-defined list of shared folders, or Not defined.

It's advisable to set this policy to a null value; there should be little impact because this null value is the default one. Any shared folders that are listed here can be accessed by any network user, which could lead to the exposure or corruption of sensitive data; leaving this list empty requires all users to be authenticated before they can access shared resources on the server.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. This setting is Not defined by default across all server types and Group Policy objects.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network access: Sharing and security model for local accounts
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines how network logons that use local accounts are authenticated.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines how network logons that use local accounts are authenticated. If you configure this setting to Classic, network logons that use local account credentials authenticate with those credentials, providing precise control over access to resources and allowing different types of access to be granted to different users for the same resource. If you configure it to Guest only, such logons are automatically mapped to the Guest account, treating all users equally with the same level of access (Read Only or Modify).

This setting doesn't affect network logons that use domain accounts, nor interactive logons performed remotely through services such as Telnet or Remote Desktop Services; when the device isn't joined to a domain, it also tailors the Sharing and Security tabs in Windows Explorer accordingly. With the Guest only model, any user who accesses the device over the network does so with Guest rights and will probably be unable to write to shared folders; with the Classic model, local accounts must be password-protected, or anyone could use them to access shared system resources.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Classic (local users authenticate as themselves) on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings, and Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy. It's advisable to keep Classic on network servers and use Guest only on end-user computers.

Choices.DisplayName: Classic - local users authenticate as themselves
Guest only - local users authenticate as Guest

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Allow Local System to use computer identity for NTLM
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether services running as Local System use the computer identity when authenticating with NTLM.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
When services connect to devices that are running versions of Windows earlier than Windows Vista or Windows Server 2008, services that run as Local System and use SPNEGO (Negotiate) that revert to NTLM will authenticate anonymously. In Windows Server 2008 R2 and Windows 7 and later, if a service connects to a computer running Windows Server 2008 or Windows Vista, the system service uses the computer identity. When a service connects with the device identity, signing and encryption are supported to provide data protection; when connecting anonymously, a system-generated session key provides no protection but allows applications to sign and encrypt data without errors.

If you enable this setting, services running as Local System that use Negotiate will use the computer identity — this is the default behavior starting with Windows Server 2008 R2 and Windows 7, but it might cause some authentication requests to Windows Server 2008/Vista systems to fail. If you disable it, such services will authenticate anonymously when falling back to NTLM, which is the default behavior on Windows Server 2008 and Windows Vista. If you configure neither, behavior differs by version: anonymous authentication on Windows Server 2008/Vista, computer identity used from Windows Server 2008 R2/Windows 7 onward.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and on Stand-Alone Server and Client Computer effective settings; it is Not applicable on Domain Controller and Member Server effective settings. Note: if Network security: Allow LocalSystem NULL session fallback is enabled, it allows NTLM or Kerberos authentication when a system service attempts authentication, which improves interoperability at the expense of security.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Allow LocalSystem NULL session fallback
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether NTLM falls back to a NULL session when used with Local System.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy affects session security during the authentication process between devices running Windows Server 2008 R2 and Windows 7 or later and devices running earlier versions of Windows. On computers running Windows Server 2008 R2 and Windows 7 or later, services running as Local System require a service principal name (SPN) to generate the session key; however, if Network security: Allow Local System to use computer identity for NTLM is disabled, these services fall back to NULL session authentication when transmitting data to servers running earlier than Windows Vista/Windows Server 2008. A NULL session doesn't establish a unique session key per authentication and therefore can't provide integrity or confidentiality protection; this setting determines whether services requesting session security are allowed to perform signature or encryption functions with a well-known key, for application compatibility.

If you enable this setting, connecting with a NULL session generates a system session key that provides no protection but allows applications to sign and encrypt data without errors, improving compatibility at the expense of security.
