If you disable it, session security is unavailable for NULL sessions and calls requesting encryption or signing will fail — a more secure configuration, but at the risk of application incompatibility; calls using the device identity retain full use of session security. If this setting isn't defined, it defaults to Enabled on versions earlier than Windows Server 2008 R2/Windows 7, and Disabled on later versions.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and on Stand-Alone Server effective settings; it is Not applicable on Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings. This policy applies to Windows Server 2008 and Windows Vista (SP1 or later); it should be disabled once your environment no longer needs to support Windows NT 4, and it's disabled by default starting with Windows 7/Windows Server 2008 R2.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Allow PKU2U authentication requests to this computer to use online identities
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the PKU2U peer-to-peer authentication protocol can use online identities.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Since Windows Server 2008 R2 and Windows 7, the Negotiate Security Support Provider (SSP) supports an extension SSP, Negoexts.dll, which is treated as an authentication protocol by Windows and supports Microsoft SSPs including PKU2U. When devices are configured to accept authentication requests using online IDs, Negoexts.dll calls the PKU2U SSP on the computer used to sign in, which obtains a local certificate and exchanges the policy between peer computers; once validated, the certificate within the metadata is sent to the sign-in peer for validation, associating the user's certificate with a security token to complete sign-in.

If you enable this setting, authentication can successfully complete between two or more computers that have established a peer relationship using online IDs. If you disable it, online IDs can no longer be used to authenticate the user to another computer in a peer relationship. If the setting isn't configured, online IDs also can't be used to authenticate — this is the default on domain-joined devices; within a domain, domain accounts should be used for authentication instead. Note: PKU2U is disabled by default on Windows Server; if disabled, Remote Desktop connections from a Microsoft Entra hybrid-joined server to a Microsoft Entra joined Windows 10 device may fail, and PKU2U must then be enabled on both the server and the client.

No restart requirement is documented for this setting. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, Disabled on Domain Controller and Member Server effective settings and on client computers prior to Windows 10 version 1607, and Enabled on client computers from Windows 10 version 1607 onward.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Configure encryption types allowed for Kerberos
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Bitmask (sum of the AES128/AES256/RC4/DES flags) determining the allowed Kerberos encryption types.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting allows you to set the encryption types that the Kerberos protocol is allowed to use; an unselected type isn't allowed. This setting can affect compatibility with client computers, services, or applications, and multiple selections are permitted. The available types are DES_CBC_CRC and DES_CBC_MD5 (supported through Windows Server 2008/Vista, not supported by default from Windows 7/Windows Server 2008 R2 onward), RC4_HMAC_MD5 (broadly supported, including by recent versions), AES128_HMAC_SHA1 and AES256_HMAC_SHA1 (not supported before Windows Vista/Windows Server 2008, supported thereafter), and a reservation for future encryption types.

It's advisable to analyze your environment to determine which encryption types will be supported and then select the types that meet that evaluation. DES suites are no longer supported by default on recent systems because stronger suites are available; enabling them allows Kerberos interoperability with non-Windows implementations of the protocol, but may open attack vectors. It's advisable not to configure this policy, which forces recent computers to use AES or RC4 suites; selecting no encryption types can cause Kerberos authentication failures with non-Windows systems, while selecting a type lowers encryption effectiveness but improves interoperability with older Windows versions.

No restart requirement is documented for this setting. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy; on domain controllers, member servers, and client computers, the default operating system setting applies and DES suites aren't supported by default.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a new LAN Manager (LM) password hash is stored the next time the password is changed.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines whether LAN Manager is prevented from storing hash values for the new password the next time the password is changed. A hash value is a representation of the password after the encryption algorithm is applied; the LAN Manager (LM) hash is relatively weak and prone to attack compared to the cryptographically stronger NTLM hash, and because it's stored locally in the security database, passwords can be compromised if the Security Accounts Manager (SAM) is attacked.

If you enable this setting, the LM hash is no longer stored on the next password change, which makes it much more difficult for an attacker who has accessed the SAM file to recover passwords using a password-cracking tool, even though it doesn't fully prevent this type of attack. If you disable or do not configure this setting, LM hashes continue to be stored on password changes, leaving this vulnerability open.

It's advisable to enable this setting and require all users to set a new password the next time they sign in to the domain, so that existing LM hashes are removed. No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings. Some non-Microsoft applications might no longer be able to connect to the system once it's enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: LAN Manager authentication level
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines which challenge/response authentication protocol is used for network logons.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines which challenge/response authentication protocol is used for network logons. In Active Directory domains, Kerberos is the default authentication protocol; however, if Kerberos isn't negotiated, Active Directory uses LM, NTLM, or NTLM version 2 (NTLMv2). LAN Manager authentication, which includes the LM, NTLM, and NTLMv2 variants, is used to authenticate Windows client devices when they join a domain, authenticate between Active Directory forests, or authenticate to older, non-Windows, or non-domain computers.

Six values are possible: Send LM & NTLM responses (registry level 0, never NTLMv2 session security); Send LM & NTLM — use NTLMv2 session security if negotiated (level 1); Send NTLM responses only (level 2); Send NTLMv2 responses only (level 3); Send NTLMv2 responses only, refuse LM (level 4, domain controllers then accept only NTLM and NTLMv2); and Send NTLMv2 responses only, refuse LM & NTLM (level 5, only NTLMv2 is accepted). This choice affects the protocol level used by clients, the session security level negotiated, and the authentication level accepted by servers.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect, but it may affect compatibility with clients, services, and applications. It's recommended to configure this setting to Send NTLMv2 responses only once all client computers support it. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy, the Default Domain Controller Policy, and on Client Computer effective settings, and Send NTLMv2 responses only on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, and Member Server effective settings. Client devices that don't support NTLMv2 authentication will then be unable to authenticate in the domain or access domain resources using LM or NTLM.

Choices.DisplayName: Send LM & NTLM - use NTLMv2 session security if negotiated
Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM
Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: LDAP client signing requirements
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines the level of data signing requested on behalf of clients issuing LDAP BIND requests.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines the level of data signing that is requested on behalf of client devices that issue LDAP BIND requests. Three levels are possible: None, where the LDAP BIND request is issued with only the caller-specified options; Negotiate signing, where, if TLS/SSL hasn't been started, the request is initiated with the LDAP signing option in addition to the caller-specified options (if TLS/SSL has been started, only the caller-specified options apply); and Require signing, the same as Negotiate signing except that if the LDAP server's intermediate saslBindInProgress response doesn't indicate that LDAP traffic signing is required, the caller receives a message that the LDAP BIND request failed.

It's advisable to set both this setting and Domain controller: LDAP server signing requirements to Require signing, to avoid the use of unsigned traffic; configuring only one side would prevent client computers from communicating with the server, which can cause many features to fail, including user authentication, Group Policy, and logon scripts.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect, but it may affect compatibility with clients, services, and applications. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Negotiate signing on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Minimum session security for NTLM SSP based (including secure RPC) clients
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Bitmask of session security requirements (128-bit encryption, NTLMv2 session security) for NTLM clients.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting allows a client device to require the negotiation of 128-bit encryption or NTLMv2 session security; these values are dependent on the Network security: LAN Manager authentication level setting. Two options exist: Require NTLMv2 session security, where the connection fails if the NTLMv2 protocol isn't negotiated, and Require 128-bit encryption, where the connection fails if strong encryption (128-bit) isn't negotiated.

Network traffic that uses the NTLM Security Support Provider (NTLM SSP) could be exposed, allowing an attacker who has gained access to the same network to create man-in-the-middle attacks; it's therefore advisable to enable all options available for this setting. However, specific practices depend on your particular security requirements.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Require 128-bit encryption on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings. Client devices that enforce these settings can't communicate with older servers that don't support them.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Minimum session security for NTLM SSP based (including secure RPC) servers
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Bitmask of session security requirements (128-bit encryption, NTLMv2 session security) for NTLM servers.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting allows a server to require the negotiation of 128-bit encryption or NTLMv2 session security; these values are dependent on the Network security: LAN Manager authentication level setting. Setting all of these values helps protect network traffic that uses the NTLM Security Support Provider (NTLM SSP) from being exposed to or tampered with by a malicious user who has gained access to the same network — that is, it helps protect against man-in-the-middle attacks.

Two options exist: Require 128-bit encryption, where the connection fails if strong encryption isn't negotiated, and Require NTLMv2 session security, where the connection fails if the NTLMv2 protocol isn't negotiated. It's advisable to enable all values available for this security policy; legacy client devices that don't support them will then be unable to communicate with the server.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Require 128-bit encryption on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings. Older client devices that don't support these security settings can't communicate with the computer on which this policy is set.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit Incoming NTLM Traffic
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether incoming NTLM traffic to this server is audited.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting allows you to audit incoming NTLM traffic. When this audit policy is enabled through Group Policy, it's enforced on any server where that Group Policy is distributed, and events are recorded in the operational event log located in Applications and Services Log\Microsoft\Windows\NTLM; only authentication traffic to that server is logged. This setting functions in the same way as Network security: Restrict NTLM: Incoming NTLM traffic, but it doesn't actually block any traffic, letting you understand the authentication traffic in your environment before enabling that other setting to block it.

Four values are possible: Disable, where no incoming NTLM traffic events are logged; Enable auditing for domain accounts, which logs NTLM pass-through authentication requests for domain accounts that would be blocked if Restrict NTLM: Incoming NTLM traffic were set to Deny all domain accounts; Enable auditing for all accounts, which logs all NTLM requests that would be blocked if that same setting were set to Deny all accounts; and Not defined, equivalent to Disable.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect; Group Policy, if defined, takes precedence over the local setting. The default value is Not defined across all server types and Group Policy objects. This setting is purely for auditing purposes: it doesn't prevent or mitigate any vulnerability by itself, but it's advisable to restrict access to the log files once enabled in production, and to monitor their size regularly.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Audit NTLM authentication in this domain
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Bitmask determining which NTLM authentications within the domain are audited (setting applies on a domain controller).
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting allows you to audit NTLM authentication in this domain on the domain controller. If you enable it on a domain controller, only authentication traffic to that domain controller is logged; it functions in the same way as Network security: Restrict NTLM: NTLM authentication in this domain, but it doesn't actually block any traffic, letting you understand the authentication traffic to your domain controllers before enabling that other setting to block it.

Five values are possible: Disable, where no events are logged; Enable for domain accounts to domain servers, which logs NTLM authentication sign-in attempts from domain accounts to domain servers that would be denied if the corresponding option were enabled in the restriction setting; Enable for domain accounts, which logs attempts using domain accounts that would similarly be denied; Enable for domain servers, which logs requests to all servers in the domain that would be denied; and Not defined, equivalent to Disable.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect; Group Policy, if defined, takes precedence over the local setting. The default value is Not defined across all server types and Group Policy objects. This setting is purely for auditing purposes and doesn't prevent or mitigate any vulnerability by itself; it's advisable to restrict access to the logs and monitor their size regularly depending on the duration of your testing.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether outgoing NTLM traffic from this computer to remote servers is allowed, audited, or denied.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting allows you to deny or audit outgoing NTLM traffic from a computer running Windows 7, Windows Server 2008 R2, or later to any remote server running Windows. Warning: modifying this setting may affect compatibility with client computers, services, and applications.

Four values are possible: Allow all, where the device can authenticate to a remote server using NTLM without restriction (same behavior as Not defined); Audit all, where the device logs an event for each NTLM authentication request sent to a remote server, letting you identify the servers involved; and Deny all, where the device can't authenticate any identity to a remote server using NTLM (an event is also logged on the requesting device) — you can then use Network security: Restrict NTLM: Add remote server exceptions for NTLM authentication to define a list of servers for which NTLM remains allowed.

Before choosing Deny all, it's advisable to first select Audit all and review the operational event log to identify the servers involved, then add them to the exception list if needed; configuring a full denial without this step can cause many NTLM authentication requests to remote servers to fail and hurt productivity. No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect; Group Policy, if defined, takes precedence over the local setting. The default value is Not defined across all server types and Group Policy objects.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Shutdown: Allow system to be shut down without having to log on
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a computer can be shut down without having to log on to Windows.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines whether a device can be shut down without having to sign in to Windows. If you enable it, the Shut Down option is available on the sign-in screen; if you disable it, that option is removed from the sign-in screen and the user must have signed in successfully and hold the Shut down the system user right in order to shut down the device.

Users with local access to the console can shut down the system; attackers or misguided users could connect to the server using Remote Desktop Services and then shut it down or restart it without having to identify themselves, or cause a temporary denial-of-service condition by restarting or shutting down the server from the local console. It's advisable to disable this setting on servers — requiring sign-in to shut them down or restart them — and to enable it on client devices, defining the list of authorized users through the Shut down the system User Rights Assignment policy.

No computer restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect, whether saved locally or distributed through Group Policy. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, Disabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, and Member Server effective settings, and Enabled on Client Computer effective settings.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: System objects: Require case insensitivity for non-Windows subsystems
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether case insensitivity is enforced for all subsystems when looking up system objects (directories, files).
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines whether case insensitivity is enforced for all subsystems. The Microsoft Win32 subsystem isn't case sensitive; however, the kernel supports case sensitivity for other subsystems, such as the Portable Operating System Interface for UNIX (POSIX). Because Windows is case insensitive but the POSIX subsystem supports case sensitivity, if this setting isn't enforced, a user of that subsystem could create a file with the same name as another file but with a different mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, potentially confusing users who try to access these files using normal Win32 tools, since only one of the files will be visible.

If you enable this setting, case insensitivity is enforced for all directory objects, symbolic links, and input/output objects, including file objects. If you disable it, the Win32 subsystem isn't allowed to become case sensitive (this doesn't in itself enable case sensitivity for other subsystems). It's advisable to enable this setting, while keeping in mind that it may confuse users familiar with case-sensitive UNIX-based operating systems.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: System objects: Strengthen default permissions of internal system objects (e.g. Symbolic Links)
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines the strength of the default discretionary access control list (DACL) for objects, letting non-admin users read but not modify shared objects they did not create.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines the strength of the default discretionary access control list (DACL) for objects. Windows maintains a global list of shared system resources such as MS-DOS device names, mutexes, and semaphores, which processes use to locate and share objects; each type of object is created with a default DACL that specifies who can access it and with what permissions.

If you enable this setting, the default DACL is strengthened, allowing users who aren't administrators to read, but not modify, shared objects that they didn't create — protecting against a known vulnerability that can be exploited using hard links or symbolic links: a malicious user could otherwise destroy a data file by creating a link with a predictable name (such as a sequentially named log file that the system creates automatically) but pointing at the target file, so that writing the expected file overwrites the targeted data. If you disable this setting, this strengthened protection isn't applied.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. It's advisable to enable this setting. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings; this default state has no impact.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Admin Approval Mode for the Built-in Administrator account
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines the behavior of Admin Approval Mode for the built-in Administrator account.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines the behavior of Admin Approval Mode for the built-in administrator account. When Admin Approval Mode is enabled, the local administrator account functions like a standard user account, but it can elevate privileges without having to log on using a different account; any operation that requires elevation of privilege then displays a prompt allowing the administrator to permit or deny that elevation. If Admin Approval Mode isn't enabled, the built-in Administrator account runs all applications by default with full administrative privileges. Note: if a computer is upgraded from a previous version of Windows and the Administrator account is the only account present, the built-in administrator account remains enabled, and this setting is also enabled.

If you enable this setting, the built-in administrator account logs on in Admin Approval Mode, prompting to permit or deny any privilege elevation. If you disable it (the default behavior), the built-in Administrator account runs all applications with full administrative privileges without prompting. It's recommended not to enable the built-in Administrator account on client computers and to use a standard user account with User Account Control instead; if you do need to enable it for administrative tasks, also enable Admin Approval Mode, and configure User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators in Admin Approval Mode to Prompt for consent on the secure desktop. Signing out and back in (or running gpupdate /force) is required to activate this setting after configuring it.

No device restart is required for the policy change itself to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Disabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Configure type of Admin Approval Mode
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether enhanced privilege protection (Administrator protection) is applied to Admin Approval Mode elevations.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Default: Legacy Admin Approval Mode.

This policy setting controls whether enhanced privilege protection is applied to Admin Approval Mode elevations. Two values are possible: Legacy Admin Approval Mode, where Admin Approval Mode runs the same way it always has; and Admin Approval Mode with Administrator protection, where elevations run with the additional isolation of the newer Administrator protection feature.

If you change this policy setting, the computer must be restarted for the change to take effect. This policy is only supported on Windows client (Desktop) editions, not Windows Server.

Choices.DisplayName: Admin Approval Mode with Administrator protection

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators in Admin Approval Mode
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines the behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines the behavior of the elevation prompt for accounts that have administrative credentials. Six values are possible: Elevate without prompting (assumes the administrator will permit the operation, with no further consent or credentials required — not recommended unless administrator accounts are tightly controlled and the environment is highly secure); Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop (the user enters a privileged user name and password on the secure desktop); Prompt for consent on the secure desktop (the user selects Permit or Deny on the secure desktop); Prompt for credentials (user name and password entry, outside the secure desktop); Prompt for consent (Permit/Deny choice, outside the secure desktop); and Prompt for consent for non-Windows binaries, the default value, where only non-Microsoft applications requiring elevation trigger a prompt on the secure desktop.

If the built-in Administrator account is enabled with Admin Approval Mode, you must also configure this setting to Prompt for consent on the secure desktop. Signing out and back in (or running gpupdate /force) is required to activate Admin Approval Mode after configuring it. This setting raises awareness to the administrator of operations requiring elevation and lets them block a malicious program attempting to elevate its privileges without their knowledge.

No computer restart is required for the policy change to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Prompt for consent for non-Windows binaries on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings; administrators should be made aware that they'll be prompted for consent whenever a binary attempts to run.

Choices.DisplayName: Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop
Prompt for consent on the secure desktop
Prompt for consent for non-Windows binaries

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators running with Administrator protection
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines the behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators running with Administrator protection (Enhanced Privilege Protection Mode).
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Default: Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop.

This policy setting controls the behavior of the elevation prompt for administrators running in Enhanced Privilege Protection Mode (Administrator protection). Two values are possible:

Prompt for consent on the secure desktop: When an operation requires elevation of privilege, the user is prompted on the secure desktop to select either Permit or Deny. If the user selects Permit, the operation continues elevated with enhanced privilege protection.

Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop: When an operation requires elevation of privilege, the user is prompted on the secure desktop to enter an administrative user name and password. If the user enters valid credentials, the operation continues elevated with enhanced privilege protection.

Choices.DisplayName: Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop
Prompt for consent on the secure desktop

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Allow remote logon with elevated privileges for domain users in the local Administrators group when Administrator protection is enabled
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether domain users who are members of the local Administrators group are granted elevated privileges during a remote logon while Administrator protection is enabled.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Default: Disabled.

This policy setting determines whether domain users who are members of the local Administrators group on a device are granted elevated privileges when performing a remote logon while Administrator protection is enabled. For more granular control over which specific users or groups get this behavior instead of the whole local Administrators group, use User Account Control: Allow remote logon with elevated privileges for specified domain users and groups when Administrator protection is enabled.

Disabled: Domain users who are members of the local Administrators group run without elevated privileges when performing remote logons while Administrator protection is enabled.

Enabled: Domain users who are members of the local Administrators group run with elevated privileges when performing remote logons while Administrator protection is enabled - this matches the behavior User Account Control already has without Administrator protection.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Behavior of the elevation prompt for standard users
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines the behavior of the elevation prompt for standard users.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines the behavior of the elevation prompt for standard users. Three values are possible: Automatically deny elevation requests, which returns an Access denied error message to standard users trying to perform an operation that requires elevation of privilege (most organizations running desktops as standard users configure this to reduce help desk calls); Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop, the default value, where the user is prompted on the secure desktop to enter a different user name and password; and Prompt for credentials, where this prompt appears outside the secure desktop.

It's advisable to configure this setting to Automatically deny elevation requests, which requires the user to sign in with an administrative account to run programs requiring elevation; as a security best practice, standard users shouldn't have knowledge of administrative passwords. However, if users have both standard and administrator-level accounts, it's advisable to configure Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop so they aren't tempted to always sign in with their administrator account and instead favor the standard account.

No computer restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings. Configuring Automatically deny may temporarily increase the load on IT staff while affected programs are identified and procedures are adapted to least-privilege operation.

Choices.DisplayName: Prompt for credentials on the secure desktop

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Detect application installations and prompt for elevation
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the system prompts for elevation when it detects application installation packages.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines the behavior of application installation detection for the entire system. Some software might attempt to install itself after being given permission to run — the user having granted that permission because the program was trusted — and then prompt the user to install an unknown component; this security policy provides another way to identify and stop these attempted software installations before they can do damage.

If you enable this setting, application installation packages that require an elevation of privilege to install are detected and the user is prompted for administrative credentials. If you disable it, these packages aren't detected and no prompt is shown. Installer detection is unnecessary in enterprises running standard user desktops that capitalize on delegated installation technologies like Group Policy Software Install (GPSI) or Configuration Manager, in which case this setting can be disabled; otherwise, it's advisable to enable it so standard users must provide administrative credentials before software is installed.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings. Users will then have to provide an administrative password to install programs.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Only elevate UIAccess applications that are installed in secure locations
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether applications that request to run with a UIAccess integrity level must reside in a secure location in the file system.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting enforces the requirement that apps requesting to run with a UIAccess integrity level (by marking UIAccess=true in their manifest) must reside in a secure location on the file system, limited to \Program Files\ (and subdirectories), \Windows\system32\, and \Program Files (x86)\ (and subdirectories) on 64-bit versions. Windows always enforces a PKI signature check on any interactive application requesting this integrity level, regardless of the state of this setting.

User Interface Privilege Isolation (UIPI) prevents lower-privilege applications from sending messages or installing hooks in higher-privilege processes; Microsoft UI Automation, the current accessibility model, needs to bypass these restrictions to drive elevated applications, which is done through the UIAccess attribute. If you enable this setting, an application can start with UIAccess integrity only if it resides in one of these secure locations; if you disable it, an application can obtain that integrity even outside these locations. A process started with UIAccess rights can, among other things, set the foreground window, drive any application window using SendInput, read input for all integrity levels using low-level hooks, and use AttachThreadInput to attach a thread to a higher-integrity input queue.

It's advisable to enable this setting. No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings; an application that doesn't meet these requirements then starts without UIAccess rights and can only interact with applications at the same or a lower privilege level.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Run all administrators in Admin Approval Mode
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether User Account Control (UAC) is enabled, with Admin Approval Mode for all administrators.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines the behavior of all User Account Control (UAC) policies for the entire system; this is the setting that turns UAC on or off globally.

If you enable this setting, Admin Approval Mode and all other UAC policies depend on it; changing this setting requires restarting the system. If you disable it, Admin Approval Mode and all related UAC policies are disabled, and Windows Security notifies the user that the overall security of the operating system has been reduced. If UAC isn't turned on, the security benefits and risk mitigations that depend on it aren't present on the computer.

It's advisable to enable this setting to allow all other UAC features and policies to function. The computer must be restarted before a change to this policy becomes effective, whether saved locally or distributed through Group Policy. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings. Users and administrators must learn to work with UAC prompts and adjust their work habits to use least-privilege operations.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Switch to the secure desktop when prompting for elevation
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the elevation prompt is displayed on the interactive user desktop or the secure desktop.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting determines whether the elevation request prompts on the interactive user desktop or on the secure desktop. The secure desktop presents the sign-in UI and restricts functionality and access to the system until the sign-in requirements are satisfied; its primary difference from the user desktop is that only trusted processes running as SYSTEM are allowed to run there (nothing runs at the user's privilege level), and the path from the user desktop to the secure desktop must be trusted through the entire chain.

If you enable this setting, all elevation requests go to the secure desktop by default. If you disable it, they go to the interactive user desktop. Elevation prompt dialog boxes can be spoofed, causing users to disclose their passwords to malicious software — for example by hiding the real cursor and replacing it with an offset one so that it actually points to the Allow button; the secure desktop helps protect against this kind of input and output spoofing by presenting the credentials dialog box in a protected section of memory that only trusted system processes can access.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. It's advisable to enable this setting. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings; this default state has no impact.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Virtualize file and registry write failures to per-user locations
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether application write failures to protected locations (Program Files, Windows, HKLM) are redirected to defined per-user locations, for non-UAC-compliant applications.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This policy setting enables or disables the redirection of write failures of earlier applications to defined locations in the registry and file system. This feature mitigates applications that historically ran as administrator and wrote runtime application data to %ProgramFiles%, %Windir%, %Windir%\system32, or HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\; it can be disabled for applications compliant with Windows Vista or later, where it becomes unnecessary.

If you enable this setting, application write failures are redirected at runtime to defined per-user locations, both in the file system and the registry. If you disable it, applications that write data to protected locations simply fail. If you run applications that aren't Windows Vista-compliant, it's advisable to enable this setting to prevent these older applications from writing data to unsecure locations; if you only run compliant applications, this setting can safely be disabled.

No restart is required for a change to this policy to take effect. The default value is Not defined in the Default Domain Policy and Default Domain Controller Policy, and Enabled on Stand-Alone Server, Domain Controller, Member Server, and Client Computer effective settings; this default state has no impact, since without it, older applications simply risk not writing their data to secure locations.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Devices: Allow undock without having to log on
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a portable computer can be undocked without logging on.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether a portable computer can be undocked without having to log on. If this policy is enabled, logon is not required and an external hardware eject button can be used to undock the computer. If disabled, a user must log on and have the Remove computer from docking station privilege to undock the computer.

Caution : Disabling this policy may tempt users to try and physically remove the laptop from its docking station using methods other than the external hardware eject button. Since this may cause damage to the hardware, this setting, in general, should only be disabled on laptop configurations that are physically securable.

Default: Enabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Devices: Restrict floppy access to locally logged-on user only
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether floppy disks are exclusively accessible to the interactively logged-on user.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether removable floppy media are accessible to both local and remote users simultaneously.

If this policy is enabled, it allows only the interactively logged-on user to access removable floppy media. If this policy is enabled and no one is logged on interactively, the floppy can be accessed over the network.

Default: This policy is not defined and floppy disk drive access is not restricted to the locally logged-on user.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Devices: Restrict CD-ROM access to locally logged-on user only
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether CD-ROM media is exclusively accessible to the interactively logged-on user.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether a CD-ROM is accessible to both local and remote users simultaneously.

If this policy is enabled, it allows only the interactively logged-on user to access removable CD-ROM media. If this policy is enabled and no one is logged on interactively, the CD-ROM can be accessed over the network.

Default: Not Defined.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Devices: Allowed to format and eject removable media
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines which group of users may format and eject removable NTFS media.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
Default: This policy is not defined and only Administrators have this ability.

This security setting determines who is allowed to format and eject removable NTFS media. This capability can be given to:

Administrators
Administrators and Interactive Users

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the virtual memory pagefile is cleared when the system shuts down.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Shutdown: Clear virtual memory pagefile
Audit: Audit the access of global system objects
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a default SACL is applied to system objects such as mutexes, events, and semaphores so their access can be audited.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether to audit the access of global system objects.

If this policy is enabled, it causes system objects, such as mutexes, events, semaphores and DOS devices, to be created with a default system access control list (SACL). Only named objects are given a SACL; SACLs are not given to objects without names.  If the Audit object access audit policy is also enabled, access to these system objects is audited.

Note: When configuring this security setting, changes will not take effect until you restart Windows.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether UIAccess (accessibility) programs can automatically disable the secure desktop for elevation prompts.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Allow UIAccess applications to prompt for elevation without using the secure desktop

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Enforces PKI signature checks on any interactive application that requests elevation of privilege.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: User Account Control: Only elevate executables that are signed and validated

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Requires users to sign in to a device using either a smart card or a Windows Hello for Business method.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Require Windows Hello for Business or smart card
Interactive logon: Don't display username at sign-in
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Prevents the username from being displayed at sign-in and immediately after credentials are entered, for the Other user tile.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the username of the person signing in to this PC appears at Windows sign-in, after credentials are entered, and before the PC desktop is shown.
If this policy is enabled, the username will not be shown.

If this policy is disabled, the username will be shown.

Default: Disabled.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Interactive logon: Machine account lockout threshold
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Number of failed sign-in attempts (BitLocker-protected devices) that will invalidate the TPM protector and force a reboot; 0 disables lockout.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines the number of failed logon attempts that causes the machine to reboot. Machines with Bitlocker enabled for protecting OS volumes will be locked out and can only be recovered by providing a recovery key at console. Please ensure that the appropriate recovery policies are enabled.

You can set the value between 1 and 999 failed logon attempts. If you set the value to 0, the machine will never be locked out. Values from 1 to 3 will be interpreted as 4.

Failed password attempts against workstations or member servers that have been locked using either CTRL+ALT+DELETE or password protected screen savers counts as failed logon attempts.

Default: 0.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Accounts: Block Microsoft accounts
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether users can add new Microsoft accounts, or add and sign in with Microsoft accounts, on this computer.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This setting prevents using the Settings app to add a Microsoft account for single sign-on (SSO) authentication for Microsoft services and some background services, or using a Microsoft account for single sign-on to other applications or services.

There are two options if this setting is enabled:

• Users can't add Microsoft accounts means that existing connected accounts can still sign in to the device (and appear on the Sign in screen). However, users cannot use the Settings app to add new connected accounts (or connect local accounts to Microsoft accounts).

• Users can't add or log on with Microsoft accounts means that users cannot add new connected accounts (or connect local accounts to Microsoft accounts) or use existing connected accounts through Settings.

This setting does not affect adding a Microsoft account for application authentication. For example, if this setting is enabled, a user can still provide a Microsoft account for authentication with an application such as Mail, but the user cannot use the Microsoft account for single sign-on authentication for other applications or services (in other words, the user will be prompted to authenticate for other applications or services).

Default : Not defined.

Choices.DisplayName: This policy is disabled and users can use Microsoft accounts with Windows
Users can't add new Microsoft accounts
Users can't add or log on with Microsoft accounts

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain controller: Allow computer account re-use during domain join
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Defines (in SDDL format) which security principals are allowed to reuse an existing computer account when joining a device to the domain.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the domain controller will allow a client identity to attempt to re-use an existing computer account owned by a different identity during domain join.

By default, the following owners are trusted: Administrators and the user performing the domain join.
When this policy is configured with a list of trusted users or groups, the domain controller will allow a client to re-use a computer account that is owned by a member of the specified group or specified identity during domain join.

This policy should be applied to all domain controllers in a domain by enabling the policy on the Domain Controllers OU.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Domain controller: Allow vulnerable Netlogon secure channel connections
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Defines a list of machine accounts allowed to use a Netlogon secure channel without secure RPC (Netlogon CVE-2020-1472 mitigation exception list).
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Explain:
This security setting determines whether the domain controller bypasses secure RPC for Netlogon secure channel connections for specified machine accounts.

This policy should be applied to all domain controllers in a forest by enabling the policy on the domain controllers OU.

When the Create Vulnerable Connections list (allow list) is configured:
    -  Given allow permission, the domain controller will allow accounts to use a Netlogon secure channel without secure RPC.
    -  Given deny permission, the domain controller will require accounts to use a Netlogon secure channel with secure RPC which is the same as the default (not necessary).

Warning! Enabling this policy will expose your domain-joined devices and can expose your Active Directory forest to risk. This policy should be used as a temporary measure for 3rd party devices as you deploy updates. Once a 3rd party device is updated to support using secure RPC with Netlogon secure channels, the account should be removed from the Create Vulnerable Connections list. 

Default: This policy is not configured. No machines or trust accounts are explicitly exempt from secure RPC with Netlogon secure channel connections enforcement.

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Defines a list of NetBIOS server names in this domain to which NTLM pass-through authentication remains allowed.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Add server exceptions in this domain

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Defines a list of remote server NetBIOS names to which this computer is still allowed to send NTLM authentication.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Add remote server exceptions for NTLM authentication
Network security: Restrict NTLM: NTLM authentication in this domain
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Allows the domain controller to deny or allow NTLM pass-through authentication within the domain.

Choices.DisplayName: Deny for domain accounts to domain servers

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Network security: Restrict NTLM: Incoming NTLM traffic
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether this server denies incoming NTLM authentication requests.
Forces the system to use only FIPS 140 validated cryptographic algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: System cryptography: Use FIPS compliant algorithms for encryption, hashing, and signing

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether the Recovery Console automatically logs on as Administrator without requiring a password.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Recovery console: Allow automatic administrative logon

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Makes the Recovery Console SET command available, allowing configuration of its related environment variables.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: Recovery console: Allow floppy copy and access to all drives and all folders
System cryptography: Force strong key protection for user keys stored on the computer
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether a password is required to use private/user keys (e.g. S/MIME keys) stored on the computer.

Choices.DisplayName: User input is not required when new keys are stored and used
User is prompted when the key is first used
User must enter a password each time they use a key

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Determines whether digital certificates are processed when a user or process attempts to run software with a .exe file extension.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: System settings: Use Certificate Rules on Windows Executables for Software Restriction Policies

SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.Description: Lists which non-Windows subsystems (e.g. POSIX) are permitted to run on the computer.
SecurityOptionsRegistryCatalog.DisplayName: System settings: Optional subsystems

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether system events are audited (startup/shutdown, system time, security log...).
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit system events policy setting determines whether Windows audits events such as a user restarting or shutting down the computer, or events that affect system security or the security log itself (for example, clearing the security log, or the loss of audit events due to an internal resource shortage).

When this setting is defined, you can independently choose to audit successes, audit failures, both, or neither. Success audits record an entry when the relevant system event completes successfully; failure audits record an entry when it fails. To configure no auditing at all, the "Define these policy settings" checkbox must remain selected with both Success and Failure cleared, rather than left "Not defined."

Default value: Success is audited on domain controllers; no auditing occurs on member servers.

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether each instance of a user logging on to or off from this computer is audited.
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit logon events policy setting determines whether Windows audits each instance of a user logging on to or logging off from a device, as recorded on that device itself (as opposed to Audit account logon events, which records domain-level authentication on the domain controller). This includes sign-ins, sign-offs, network logons, and disconnected Terminal Services sessions.

If both this policy and Audit account logon events are enabled, a domain-account interactive logon to a workstation or member server generates a logon event on that computer and an account logon event on the domain controller that validated the credentials. When this setting is defined, success audits, failure audits, both, or neither can be selected independently; success audits record a successful logon or logoff, while failure audits record a failed logon attempt.

Default value: Success is audited on domain controllers; no auditing occurs on member servers.

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether access to an object (file, registry key...) that has its own system access control list is audited.
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit object access policy setting determines whether Windows audits the event of a user accessing an object—such as a file, folder, registry key, or printer—that has its own system access control list (SACL) configured. Simply enabling this policy is not enough by itself: a SACL must also be defined on the specific object, through the Security tab of its Properties dialog box, before any access to it will be logged.

When this setting is defined, success audits, failure audits, both, or neither can be selected independently. A success audit records an entry when a user successfully accesses an object that has an appropriate SACL; a failure audit records an entry when such an access attempt is denied.

Default value: No auditing.

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether the use of a user right is audited.
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit privilege use policy setting determines whether Windows audits each instance of a user exercising a user right (privilege), such as changing the system time or taking ownership of a file.

When this setting is defined, success audits, failure audits, both, or neither can be selected independently: a success audit records an entry when the exercise of a right succeeds, and a failure audit records an entry when it fails. A handful of very frequently used rights—including Bypass traverse checking, Debug programs, Create a token object, Replace a process level token, Generate security audits, Back up files and directories, and Restore files and directories—are excluded from this auditing by default, because logging them would generate an excessive volume of events; auditing these specific rights requires separately enabling the FullPrivilegeAuditing registry key.

Default value: No auditing.

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether every incident of a change to user rights assignment, audit, or trust policies is audited.
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit policy change policy setting determines whether Windows audits every change to user rights assignment policies, audit policies, or trust policies (relationships with other domains or forests).

When this setting is defined, success audits, failure audits, both, or neither can be selected independently. A success audit records an entry when a change to a rights, audit, or trust policy succeeds—for example, a user right being assigned or removed, an audit policy being modified, or a trust relationship being created, modified, or removed; a failure audit records an entry when such a change attempt fails.

Default value: Success is audited on domain controllers; no auditing occurs on member servers.

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether every account management event on a computer is audited.
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit account management policy setting determines whether Windows audits each account management event on a device, such as a user or group account being created, changed, deleted, renamed, disabled, or enabled, or a password being set or changed.

When this setting is defined, success audits, failure audits, both, or neither can be selected independently. A success audit records an entry when an account management action succeeds; a failure audit records an entry when it fails.

Default value: Success is audited on domain controllers; no auditing occurs on member servers.

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether detailed tracking information is audited (program activation, process exit...).
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit process tracking policy setting determines whether Windows audits detailed tracking information for events such as program activation, process termination, handle duplication, and indirect object access.

When this setting is defined, success audits, failure audits, both, or neither can be selected independently. A success audit records an entry when the tracked process event succeeds; a failure audit records an entry when it fails. Because this category can generate a very large number of events, it is typically left disabled except for targeted troubleshooting or forensic investigation.

Default value: No auditing.

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether a user accessing an Active Directory object that has its own system access control list is audited.
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit directory service access policy setting determines whether Windows audits the event of a user accessing an Active Directory object that has its own system access control list (SACL) configured. It is the Active Directory equivalent of Audit object access, applying specifically to directory objects rather than to file system or registry objects; a SACL must be set on the specific directory object, through the Security tab of its Properties dialog box, before accesses to it are logged.

When this setting is defined, success audits, failure audits, both, or neither can be selected independently. A success audit records an entry when a user successfully accesses a SACL-protected Active Directory object; a failure audit records an entry when such an access attempt fails. This setting has no meaning on workstations and member servers, since they do not host a directory service.

Default value: Success is audited on the Default Domain Controller Policy; undefined (no meaning) on member servers.

AuditPolicyCatalog.Description: Determines whether each instance of credential validation for an account is audited.
AuditPolicyCatalog.Explain:
The Audit account logon events policy setting determines whether Windows audits each instance of a user logging on to or logging off from another device that uses this device to validate the account. Account logon events are generated on a domain controller whenever it authenticates a domain account, and on a local computer whenever it authenticates a local account; account logoff events are not generated at all.

This setting complements Audit logon events: the latter records the logon/logoff activity on the computer where the interactive session actually takes place, while this setting records the underlying authentication (for example, Kerberos ticket issuance and validation) on the computer that verified the credentials. When this setting is defined, success audits, failure audits, both, or neither can be selected independently.

Default value: Success.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Access this computer from the network
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This user right determines which users and computers can connect to this device over the network. It is required by many network protocols, including SMB, NetBIOS, CIFS, and COM+, and is what allows a remote user to reach shared folders, printers, and other resources hosted on this computer.

Users who can connect over the network can access any resource on the device for which they have permissions. If this right were granted to the Everyone group, anyone in that group could read the contents of shared folders that grant Everyone read access; this risk is mitigated by default because modern Windows installations do not include Everyone in this right, but upgraded systems may still carry it over.

Default on workstations and servers:
Administrators
Backup Operators
Users
Everyone

Default on domain controllers:
Administrators
Authenticated Users
Enterprise Domain Controllers
Everyone
Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access

This right determines which users can bypass file, directory, registry, and other persistent-object permissions for the sole purpose of backing up the system; it only takes effect when an application accesses objects through the NTFS backup API (such as through a dedicated backup tool), not through ordinary file access. Granting it is functionally equivalent to giving the account Traverse Folder/Execute File, List Folder/Read Data, Read Attributes, Read Extended Attributes, and Read Permissions on every file and folder on the system.

Anyone who can back up data from a computer could carry the backup media to a non-domain machine where they have administrative rights, restore the data there, take ownership of the files, and view any information that was not encrypted.

Default : On workstations and servers: Administrators, Backup Operators.
Default : On domain controllers:Administrators, Backup Operators, Server Operators

This right lets a user (or a process acting on the user's behalf) navigate through an NTFS or registry path without being checked for the Traverse Folder special permission on each intermediate folder; it does not let the user list a folder's contents, only pass through it to reach a file or subfolder they already have permission to access.

By default this right is granted to Everyone, which is intentional: since traversal alone grants no read or write access, the only realistic risk is an administrator mistakenly assuming that blocking access to a parent folder also blocks access to its children, which is a low-probability configuration error.

Default : On workstations and servers: Administrators, Backup Operators, Users, Everyone, Local Service, Network Service
Default : On domain controllers: Administrators, Authenticated Users, Everyone, Local Service, Network Service, Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access

This right determines who can adjust the device's internal clock, changing the date and time recorded in event logs, file timestamps, and database transactions; it does not affect the ability to change the time zone, which is governed separately.

Users who can change the system time can make event log entries inaccurate, corrupt file timestamps, and — because Kerberos requires client and server clocks to stay within an administrator-defined skew — cause authentication failures if the clock is pushed out of tolerance. This risk grows significantly if an attacker who can change the time also stops or reconfigures the Windows Time service to synchronize with an inaccurate time source.

Default : On workstations and servers: Administrators, Local Service
Default : On domain controllers: Administrators, Server Operators, Local Service

This right determines who can change the time zone the device uses to display local time — the combination of the system's underlying (UTC-based) time plus a zone offset — without touching the underlying system time itself.

Changing the time zone represents very little security risk, since the system time is unaffected; the setting simply lets users display the time in the zone that is convenient to them, even while their clock stays synchronized with domain controllers in other zones. No countermeasure is generally necessary.

Default: Administrators, Users

This right determines who can create a page file (pagefile.sys) or change its size, whether through the Performance Options dialog in System Properties or through internal APIs; Windows uses the page file to supplement physical RAM for frequently used data.

A user who can change the page file's size could shrink it excessively or relocate it to a heavily fragmented volume, degrading system performance.

Default: Administrators.

This right lets a process create an access token — using NtCreateToken() or similar APIs — that it can then use to gain access to local resources, effectively letting the process manufacture credentials rather than obtain them through a normal logon.

Any account granted this right has complete control over the system and could compromise it entirely, since Windows relies on the access token to determine a user's level of privilege; someone who can create or modify tokens can grant any account any level of access, escalate their own privileges, or trigger a denial-of-service condition. Microsoft strongly advises never assigning this right to any user account.

Default : None.

This right determines who can create objects that are global — visible and usable by any process or thread on the system, even ones outside the creator's own session — as opposed to objects scoped only to the creator's session, which any user can create without this right. Remote Desktop Services relies on global objects internally to manage its connections.

A user who can create global objects can affect processes running in other users' sessions, which can lead to application failures or data corruption.

Default: Administrators, Local Service, Network Service, Service

This right determines which accounts a process can use to create a directory object in the object manager — including permanent shared objects such as devices, semaphores, and mutexes. Kernel-mode components, which extend the object namespace, already carry this right inherently and never need it assigned explicitly.

Anyone with this right could create new shared objects and inadvertently expose sensitive data over the network.

Default: None.

This right determines whether a user can create a symbolic link — a file system object that transparently points to another file or folder (its target) — from the device they are signed in to; Windows implements symbolic links to behave like their UNIX counterparts, mainly to aid migration and compatibility.

Users with this right could inadvertently or deliberately expose the system to symbolic-link attacks, which can be used to alter file permissions, corrupt or destroy data, or cause a denial of service, particularly against applications that were not written to handle links safely.

Default: Administrator

This right determines who can attach a debugger to any process — even one they do not own, including sensitive system processes — and provides access to critical, sensitive operating-system components; developers debugging their own applications do not need it, but those debugging new system components do.

Because it grants such deep access, this right can be exploited to capture sensitive information straight from system memory. Attack tools have used it to extract password hashes and other private security information; the fact that Windows assigns it only to Administrators by default significantly limits this risk.

Remove this right from any account that does not need it. If debugging is required temporarily on a production server, it is preferable to move that server into a separate organizational unit and assign the right there rather than leave it broadly granted.

Default: Administrators

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Deny access to this computer from the network
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right determines which users are explicitly blocked from accessing the device over the network, and it takes precedence over the Access this computer from the network right whenever an account is subject to both.

Users who can sign in over the network can enumerate account names, group names, and shared resources, and — if they hold permission on shared folders and files — connect and possibly view or modify data. Denying this right to high-risk accounts adds a layer of protection.

Assign this right to Anonymous Logon, the built-in local Administrator account, the local Guest account, and all service accounts — except any service account that itself needs to reach the computer over the network (for example, an account running IIS that must access a shared folder remotely). 

Default: Guest

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Deny log on as a batch job
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right blocks the accounts it is assigned to from signing in through a batch-queue tool used to schedule and start jobs automatically, such as Task Scheduler; it takes precedence over the Log on as a batch job right when an account is subject to both.

Accounts that can sign in as a batch job could be used to schedule tasks that consume excessive system resources and cause a denial-of-service condition.

Assign this right to the local Guest account. Assigning it to accounts that legitimately need to run scheduled tasks — including administrators who use their personal accounts for that purpose — will prevent those tasks from running, so changes should be tested carefully.

Default: None.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Deny log on as a service
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right blocks the accounts it is assigned to from signing in as a service application; it takes precedence over the Log on as a service right when an account is subject to both.

Accounts that can sign in as a service could be used to configure and start new, unauthorized services such as a keylogger or other malware; this risk is somewhat offset by the fact that only accounts with administrative rights can install and configure services in the first place, and an attacker at that level could simply configure a service to run as Local System instead.

Microsoft recommends not assigning this right to any account by default. Organizations with strong security concerns may assign it to groups and accounts they are certain will never need to run as a service, but assigning it broadly can prevent services from starting and cause a denial-of-service condition.

Default: None.

This right blocks the accounts it is assigned to from signing in directly at the device's console; it takes precedence over the Allow log on locally right when an account is subject to both, and applying it to the Everyone group would prevent anyone from signing in locally.

Any account that can sign in locally can be used at the console of the device; failing to restrict this right to legitimate users who need console access could let unauthorized users download and run malicious software to elevate their privileges.

Assign this right to the local Guest account, and to any other accounts that pose a comparable risk. If optional components such as ASP.NET are installed, this right may need to be assigned to their service accounts as well. 

Default: None.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Deny log on through Remote Desktop Services
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right blocks the accounts it is assigned to from signing in to the device through a Remote Desktop Services connection; it takes precedence over the Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services right when an account is subject to both.

Any account that can sign in through Remote Desktop Services can reach the remote console of the device; if this right isn't restricted to legitimate users who need console access, unauthorized users could download and run software to elevate their privileges.

Assign this right to the built-in local Guest account and to all service accounts. If optional components such as ASP.NET are installed, this right may also need to be assigned to their accounts.

Default: None.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Enable computer and user accounts to be trusted for delegation
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right determines who can set the Trusted for Delegation flag on a user or computer object in Active Directory, enabling authentication delegation — the mechanism multi-tier client/server applications use so a front-end service can reuse a client's credentials to authenticate to a back-end service. Only administrators holding this right can configure delegation, and the account granted the right must also have write access to the object's account-control flags.

Misuse of this right could allow unauthorized users to impersonate other users on the network, letting an attacker reach network resources under someone else's identity and making incidents much harder to reconstruct afterward.

Grant this right only when there is a clear operational need, and consider using constrained delegation to limit what delegated accounts can actually do. It has no meaning on member servers or domain-joined workstations — it is only relevant on domain controllers and stand-alone systems.

Default: On domain controller : Administrators.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Force shutdown from a remote system
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right determines who can shut down a device from a remote location on the network, allowing administrators or designated staff to manage computers — for example to restart them — without being physically present.

Any user who can shut down a device remotely can cause a denial-of-service condition, so this right should be tightly restricted.

Restrict it to members of the Administrators group, or to other specific roles that genuinely require this capability, such as non-administrative operations staff. 

Default: On workstations and servers: Administrators.
Default: On domain controllers: Administrators, Server Operators.

This right determines which accounts a process can use to generate audit records in the security event log, which the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) writes to and which can be used to trace unauthorized access to the device.

A malicious user with write access to the security log could fill it with meaningless entries; if the computer is set to overwrite old events as needed, this can be used to erase evidence of unauthorized activity, and if the computer is instead set to shut down when it cannot write to the log, the same technique can be turned into a denial-of-service attack.
