Ensure only the Local Service and Network Service accounts hold this right, which is the default configuration. 

Default: Local Service, Network Service.

This right determines which programs can impersonate a user or another specified account and act on the user's behalf after that user has authenticated; requiring this right for impersonation prevents an unauthorized user from tricking a client into connecting (for example over RPC or a named pipe) to a service they created, then impersonating that client to escalate to administrative or system-level access. Services started by the Service Control Manager, and COM servers configured to run under a specific account, receive this right automatically through the built-in Service group added to their access tokens.

An attacker who holds this right could create a service, lure a client into connecting to it, and then impersonate that client to elevate their own level of access to that of the device.

On member servers, ensure only the Administrators group and the Service groups (Local Service, Network Service, Service) hold this right, which is the default configuration; if optional components such as IIS or ASP.NET are installed, they may need this right assigned to their own accounts (for example IUSR or IIS_IUSRS). 

Default: Administrators, Local Service, Network Service, Service

This right determines which users can increase or decrease the working set of a process — the set of memory pages currently resident in physical RAM and immediately usable without triggering a page fault — which in turn affects the process's virtual-memory paging behavior.

Increasing a process's working set reduces the amount of physical memory left available to the rest of the system, which can degrade overall performance if used carelessly.

Make users aware of the performance impact of changing this setting and how to recognize when their system has been adversely affected. 

Default: Users

This right determines which accounts can raise the base priority class of a process — increasing a process's relative priority within its own class is not a privileged operation and does not require this right. It is not needed by the administrative tools included with Windows but may be required by software development tools; a user who holds it can change a process's scheduling priority from the Task Manager interface.

A user with this right could raise a process's priority to Real-Time, leaving very little processing time for every other process and potentially causing a denial-of-service condition.

Default: Administrators (and, on later Windows versions, also to the built-in Window Manager\Window Manager Group account)

This right determines which users can dynamically load and unload device drivers, which run as highly privileged code with essentially unrestricted access to the entire computer; it is not needed if a signed driver for the new hardware is already present in driver.cab.

A user with this right could unintentionally install malware disguised as a device driver, since driver code runs with the same trust as the operating system itself.

Default on workstations and servers: Administrators.
Default on domain controllers: Administrators, Print Operators

This right determines which accounts can use a process to keep data resident in physical memory, preventing Windows from paging that data out to disk; enabling it for an account can noticeably degrade overall system performance because it limits how much memory Windows can reclaim under pressure.

Users with this right could pin physical memory across several processes, leaving little or no RAM for everything else and causing a denial-of-service condition.

Do not assign this right to any account.

Default: None.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Log on as a batch job
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right determines which accounts can sign in using a batch-queue tool such as the Task Scheduler service. When an administrator uses the Scheduled Task wizard to run a task under a specific user name and password, that user is automatically granted this right; at the scheduled time, Task Scheduler signs the user in as a batch job rather than interactively, and the task runs in that user's security context.

This right presents a low-risk vulnerability that lets non-administrators perform administrator-like functions; if not properly assessed and restricted, it can be exploited to compromise systems, credentials, or data, though for most organizations the default configuration is sufficient.

Let the system manage this right automatically for accounts used with the Task Scheduler; if you do not use the Task Scheduler this way, restrict the right to the Local Service account.

Default: Administrators, Backup Operators.

This right determines which service accounts can register a process as a service, letting it run continuously without requiring a user to be signed in or any human intervention.

This right allows accounts to start network services or services that run even when nobody is signed in at the console; the risk is reduced because only accounts with administrative privileges can install and configure services in the first place, and an attacker with that level of access could simply configure the service to run as Local System instead.

The Network Service account already has this right by definition, without it being granted through Group Policy; minimize how many other accounts are granted it. 
Note : Components such as IIS are installed, their service accounts (for example ASPNET) may need it explicitly.

Default setting: Network Service.

This right determines which users can start an interactive session directly at the device; users who lack it can still start a remote interactive session if they separately hold the Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services right.

Any account with this right can sign in at the console of the device; failing to restrict it to legitimate users who need console access could let unauthorized users download and run malicious software to elevate their privileges.

Default : On workstations and servers: Administrators, Backup Operators, Power Users, Users, and Guest.
Default : On domain controllers: Account Operators, Administrators, Backup Operators, and Print Operators.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Allow log on through Remote Desktop Services
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right determines which users or groups can reach the sign-in screen of a remote device through a Remote Desktop Services connection; it is possible for a user to establish a Remote Desktop session to a server without being able to sign in at that server's own console.

Any account with this right can sign in to the remote console of the device; if it isn't restricted to legitimate users who need that access, unauthorized users could download and run malicious software to elevate their privileges.

Default: On workstation and servers: Administrators, Remote Desktop Users.
Default: On domain controllers: Administrators.

This right determines which users can specify object-access audit options for individual resources such as files, Active Directory objects, and registry keys — though object-access auditing itself only takes effect once enabled through the Audit Policy. A user holding this right can also view and clear the Security log in Event Viewer.

Anyone with this right can clear the Security log, potentially erasing important evidence of unauthorized activity.

Ensure only the local Administrators group holds this right, which is the default configuration; before removing it from any other group, verify that no applications depend on it, since doing so can otherwise cause performance issues.

Default: Administrators.

This right determines which accounts can change the Windows Integrity Control (WIC) integrity label of an object — such as a file, registry key, or process — that belongs to another user; without this right, a process can still lower the label of an object it owns, just not raise it or modify objects owned by others. Integrity levels (Untrusted, Low, Medium, High, System, and Installer) are mandatory controls enforced by the operating system, distinct from discretionary NTFS permissions.

Anyone with this right can raise or lower an object's integrity level to a point where protections offered by Windows Integrity Controls are effectively circumvented, exposing the system to attack by lower-integrity malicious software.

Do not give this right to any group by default; if it is ever required — for instance to relabel an object after malware has set itself to an elevated integrity level such as System — grant it temporarily to a trusted individual for a constrained period, and always relabel using a process running at the same or higher integrity level than the target object.

Default: None

This right determines who can modify firmware environment values — settings stored in non-volatile memory whose exact meaning depends on the boot firmware; on a UEFI-based system, for example, this NVRAM area specifies boot settings, while on legacy x86 systems the only value affected is Last Known Good Configuration. This right is also required to install or upgrade Windows on any computer.

Anyone assigned this right could configure a hardware component's settings so that it fails, potentially leading to data corruption or a denial-of-service condition.

Ensure only the local Administrators group holds this right, which is the default configuration; removing it can render BitLocker Drive Encryption inoperable. 

Default: Administrators.

This right determines which users can perform volume or disk management tasks, such as defragmenting a volume, creating or deleting volumes, or running Disk Cleanup.

Users with this right can explore disks and extend files into memory areas that contain other data; when such extended files are later opened, the user might be able to read — or modify — data they were never meant to access.

Ensure only the local Administrators group is assigned this right, which is the default configuration.

Default: Administrators

This right determines which users can sample the performance of a single application process. It is generally not needed to use the built-in Performance snap-in, but it is required if the system monitor is configured to collect data through Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI).

This right presents a moderate vulnerability: an attacker who holds it could monitor a computer's performance to identify critical processes worth attacking directly, or determine which processes are running in order to identify countermeasures — such as antivirus software or intrusion-detection systems — to avoid, and could also identify other users signed in to the computer.

Ensure only the local Administrators group is assigned this right, which is the default configuration; removing it from the Power Users group or similar accounts could limit users assigned to specific administrative roles. 

Default: Administrators.

This right determines which users can use Windows performance-monitoring tools to monitor the performance of system processes as a whole, rather than a single application.

This right poses a moderate vulnerability: an attacker who holds it could monitor a computer's performance to identify critical processes worth attacking directly, and could determine which processes are active in order to identify countermeasures to avoid, such as antivirus software or an intrusion-detection system.

Ensure only the local Administrators group is assigned this right, which is the default configuration. 

Default: Administrators (and, on later Windows versions, also to the built-in NT SERVICE\WdiServiceHost account)

This right determines whether a user can undock a portable device from its docking station without having to sign in first, using Eject PC from the Start menu; it only applies to scenarios involving a portable computer and its docking station. If the right is not assigned, a user may physically undock the device without signing in, and can then start it and sign in afterward in its undocked state.

Anyone with this right can sign in and then remove a portable device from its docking station; however, the practical value of restricting it is limited since an attacker who can restart the device could undock it after the BIOS starts but before Windows loads, and a determined attacker could simply steal the device and its docking station together. This setting normally has no relevance for servers, which are rarely docked.

Ensure only the local Administrators group and the specific user to whom the device is allocated are assigned this right. 

Default: Administrators, Users

This right determines which parent processes can replace the access token associated with a child process — specifically, which accounts can call the CreateProcessAsUser() API so that one service can start another under a different security context. Task Scheduler is a typical example, extending this right to any process it manages; every child process launched this way has its access token replaced by the primary token supplied.

Users with this right can start processes as another user if they know that user's credentials, which could be used to disguise unauthorized activity.

On member servers, ensure only the Local Service and Network Service accounts hold this right, which is the default configuration; optional components such as IIS may require it to also be granted explicitly to accounts like Service, Network Service, or IWAM_<ComputerName>. 

Default: Network Service, Local Service.

This right determines which users can bypass file, directory, registry, and other persistent-object permissions when restoring backed-up files and directories, and which users can set any valid security principal as the owner of an object. Granting it is functionally equivalent to giving the account Traverse Folder/Execute File and Write permissions on every file and folder on the system.

An attacker with this right could restore sensitive data onto a system, overwriting more recent data and causing data loss, corruption, or a denial-of-service condition; they could also overwrite legitimate executables used by administrators or system services with malicious versions to gain elevated privileges or maintain persistent access. Even with this right properly restricted, an attacker could still restore data on a different, attacker-controlled system, which is why the backup media itself must be carefully protected.

Ensure only the local Administrators group is assigned this right, unless your organization has clearly defined separate backup and restore roles. 

Default: On Workstations and servers: Administrators, Backup Operators.
Default: On Domain controllers: Administrators, Backup Operators, Server Operators.

This right determines whether a user who is signed in locally can shut down Windows; it is also required to enable hibernation support, configure power-management settings, and cancel a pending shutdown. Shutting down a domain controller makes it unable to process sign-ins, apply Group Policy, or answer LDAP queries, and shutting down a domain controller that holds an operations-master (FSMO) role can disable key domain functionality such as processing new-password requests handled by the PDC emulator.

The ability to shut down domain controllers should be limited to a small number of trusted administrators; although shutting down a server requires the ability to sign in to it in the first place, the accounts and groups allowed to do so should still be carefully controlled, especially on server roles where non-administrators are allowed to sign in, such as RD Session Host servers.

Ensure only Administrators and Backup Operators hold this right on member servers, and only Administrators on domain controllers. 

Default on Workstations: Administrators, Backup Operators, Users.
Default on Servers: Administrators, Backup Operators.
Default on Domain controllers: Administrators, Backup Operators, Server Operators, Print Operators.

This right determines which users and groups can synchronize all Active Directory directory-service data, regardless of the protection set on individual objects and properties; it is required to use LDAP directory-synchronization (DirSync) services. Domain controllers hold this right inherently, since the synchronization process runs in the context of the System account.

An attacker who holds this right can view all information stored in the directory, and could use some of it to facilitate further attacks or to expose sensitive data, such as direct phone numbers or physical addresses.

Ensure no accounts are explicitly assigned this right — only domain controllers need it, and they already have it inherently. 

Defaults: None.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Take ownership of files or other objects
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right determines which users can take ownership of any securable object on the device, including Active Directory objects, NTFS files and folders, printers, registry keys, services, processes, and threads. Every object has an owner — by default whoever created it — and the owner can always change permissions on the object, even if otherwise denied all access to it.

Any user with this right can seize control of an object regardless of the permissions set on it, then make whatever changes they want, which can lead to data exposure, data corruption, or a denial-of-service condition.

Ensure only the local Administrators group holds this right, which is the default configuration. 

Default: Administrators.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Access Credential Manager as a trusted caller
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right is used internally by Credential Manager during backup and restore operations; it is assigned only to the Winlogon service, and no ordinary account should ever be granted it.

If an account were given this right, that account could be used to build an application that calls into Credential Manager and retrieves another user's saved credentials.

Default : Not defined

This right determines which users can add a computer to a specific domain; to take effect it must apply to at least one domain controller, and a user holding it can add up to ten workstations to the domain. Users can also join computers to a domain without this right if they hold the Create Computer Objects permission on an organizational unit or the Computers container, in which case there is no limit on how many computers they can add.

This right presents a moderate vulnerability: a user who holds it could add a device to the domain in a way that violates organizational policy — for example, installing Windows on a personal computer, joining it to the domain, then adding their domain account to the local Administrators group using the local administrator credentials they control.

Default: Authenticated Users on domain controllers.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Adjust memory quotas for a process
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right determines who can change the maximum amount of memory that a process is allowed to consume; it is primarily useful for system tuning on a per-group or per-user basis.

A user with this right can reduce the memory available to any process, which could slow down or crash business-critical applications; a malicious user could exploit it to mount a denial-of-service attack.

Note : Components such as IIS may require it to be explicitly assigned to additional accounts (for example IWAM_<ComputerName>).

Default: Administrators, Local Service, Network Service.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Obtain an impersonation token for another user in the same session
UserRightsCatalog.Explain: Assigning this privilege to a user allows programs running on behalf of that user to obtain an impersonation token of other users who interactively logged on within the same session provided the caller has an impersonation token of the session user. Not applicable within desktop windows client/server where every user gets a separate session.

UserRightsCatalog.DisplayName: Act as part of the operating system
UserRightsCatalog.Explain:
This right determines whether a process can register with the Local Security Authority (LSA) as a trusted, low-level authentication service, letting it assume the identity of any user and gain access to the same resources as that user without going through normal authentication — effectively acting as part of the operating system itself. It is an extremely powerful right, rarely required outside deeply integrated system components.

Any account granted this right has complete control over the device and could compromise it entirely, since a process holding it can impersonate any user, including highly privileged ones, to gain unrestricted access to local resources; Microsoft strongly recommends never assigning it to any user account.

Default: None
